The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

#6397. Scientists Discover 15,000-Year-Old Clay Figures That Rewrite the History of Human Art

Clay figurines from the Middle East suggest that artistic traditions were already being shared across generations before farming, possibly with children taking part in their creation.

Long before agriculture transformed life in the Middle East, people were already shaping clay into figures that reflected the world around them. Some resembled birds, mammals, and humans, while others carried traces of red or orange coloring. One fragment may even depict the facial markings of a mountain gazelle.

These small artifacts, originally excavated from three sites in present-day Israel, date back roughly 15,000 to 11,500 years. Researchers believe they provide the earliest known evidence of a clay figurine-making tradition in the region, suggesting that people were using the material for symbolic expression much earlier than previously thought.

At the time, the region was home to Natufian communities, hunter-gatherers who had begun living in permanent settlements before the development of agriculture. Archaeologists already knew that Natufian people made figurines, although most previously discovered examples were fashioned from bone or stone.

Clay figurines, by contrast, were generally believed to have become common during the Neolithic period, when the agricultural revolution began around 11,500 years ago. The newly identified objects suggest that the practice had much deeper roots, revealing a wider range of artistic expression among these early communities.

The findings also raise questions about how cultural traditions developed before farming. The researchers suggest that Natufian artistic practices were more varied and complex than previously recognized, and that some aspects of the region’s later Neolithic culture may have originated thousands of years earlier.

The research, published November 11, 2026, in the open-access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Dr. Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel and colleagues. Beyond revealing an earlier history of clay figurines, the study offers clues about how creative practices and cultural knowledge may have passed between generations.

“These discoveries change how we understand the beginnings of artistic expression in the first villages of humanity. Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world. What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations,” said Davin.

Reference: “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia” by Laurent Davin, Marion Sindel, Mina Weinstein-Evron, Reuven Yeshurun, Daniel Kaufman, Leore Grosman, Anna Belfer-Cohen, Hamoudi Khalaily and François R. Valla, 11 November 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360388

#6396. Reconstructing Cosmic History and Earth's Evolution From Cosmic Explosions

When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

These include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have launched the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

The project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

First, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

Supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA

Second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. To answer these questions, researchers at the SUPREME project will search for extremely rare radioactive isotopes in lunar samples provided by NASA, deep-sea sediments, ice cores, and other geological archives. These archives preserve the history of interstellar material that arrived on Earth over eons, allowing scientists to identify and date nearby supernovae and other nearby energetic events.

Their work will build on the first detection of radioactive isotopes created by a rapid neutron-capture (r-process) event in history, the process by which about half of all atoms heavier than iron are created in the Universe. This occured in June 2026, when scientists from the HZDR made the first significant measurement of curium-247 and plutonium-244 in interstellar matter trapped on Earth. As Prof. Sebastian M. Schmidt, the Scientific Director of HZDR who led the discovery team, said in an HZDR statement:

This award is a remarkable recognition of Anton Wallner's internationally leading research. SUPREME addresses fundamental questions about the origin of the elements and the history of our cosmic environment while building on measurement capabilities that are unique worldwide. We are proud that this pioneering work is being carried out at HZDR.

To detect and measure rare radioactive isotopes, the researchers will use HAMSTER (Helmholtz Accelerator Mass Spectrometer Tracing Environmental Radionuclides), a new state-of-the-art accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) facility developed by Wallner and his team and installed at HZDR in 2025. Combined with an innovative laser-based technology that dramatically reduces measurement background, the team will be able to detect individual atoms with unprecedented sensitivity, opening new possibilities for astrophysics and other scientific applications.

The results of this project are expected to provide unprecedented insights into the history of our cosmic neighborhood and its possible influence on Earth's geology and species evolution. "Securing one of the European Union's most competitive research grants is an outstanding accomplishment," said Saxony's Minister of Science, Sebastian Gemkow. "This distinction is not only a major milestone in the recipients' scientific careers, but also a significant gain for Saxony as a leading research and innovation hub."

#6395. Tiny Grains of Sand Could Reveal What the Weather Was Like on Mars Billions of Years Ago

Scientists have discovered a surprising connection between sand grain size and the winds that shape dunes on Earth and Mars.

The size of a sand grain could reveal how fast the wind was blowing when a desert dune formed, even billions of years ago. Stanford University researchers have discovered that dunes on Earth and Mars are primarily shaped by winds traveling just above the minimum speed needed to move sand. Their findings offer a way to reconstruct ancient winds using sediment preserved in planetary landscapes.

Windblown dunes and ripples have been identified on Venus, Mars, Saturn’s moon Titan, and even a comet orbiting the sun. Their shapes and patterns provide evidence of prevailing wind directions and how consistently winds have blown, but determining wind speeds has been much more difficult.

In a study published November 16 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers demonstrated that the wind speeds responsible for most dune formation are closely linked to the median size of the sand grains. Stronger winds can transport larger particles, while finer grains generally require less force to move.

The relationship depends on a critical threshold: the wind must be strong enough to set sand grains in motion along the ground. Although faster winds can transport more sediment, the researchers found that winds only modestly exceeding this threshold account for much of the sand movement that builds dunes.

The research builds on a hypothesis proposed by University of Pennsylvania scientists in 2010, suggesting that dunes develop mainly under winds slightly stronger than those needed to initiate sand transport. “Since then, nobody’s really looked at this idea, even though it’s really powerful because it tells you something about the environmental conditions that formed the dune fields that we see on not just Earth and Mars, but on a variety of other planetary bodies,” said lead author Colin Marvin, who conducted the research as a PhD student at Stanford.

To test the idea, the team examined 30 years of wind observations alongside sand grain measurements from 24 dune fields worldwide. The sites encompassed different dune shapes, sizes, and environments, including Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah and the ancient desert landscapes of Namibia.

For each location, the researchers calculated which wind speed transported the greatest amount of sand over time. Across all 24 fields, that speed was closely associated with grain size and remained only slightly above the threshold required to move the sediment.

The team next examined measurements from a Martian dune field, where the relationship between sand size and the winds responsible for dune formation was similar to that observed on Earth. This held despite major differences in atmospheric pressure, gravity, and sediment density between the two planets.

The results suggest that the same basic process may govern dune formation on other worlds, provided loose sediment is abundant and stronger winds become progressively less frequent. Marvin described dunes as a “great recorder of what happens on a planet’s surface, and particularly the interactions between what’s happening in the atmosphere of a planet and what’s happening on the surface.”

Because sand grains can survive long after the winds that transported them have disappeared, the relationship could help scientists estimate ancient wind speeds from sedimentary rocks. It may also provide a way to test models of atmospheric circulation during periods when Earth’s atmosphere differed substantially from its present state.

The discovery could help researchers “better reconstruct winds and climates through time, on Earth and beyond,” said senior author Mathieu Lapôtre, associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. “It works for modern dunes and for sandstones dating back three billion years.”

Such reconstructions could be used to investigate the atmospheric histories of both Earth and Mars. According to Lapôtre, the research is already moving in that direction. “Colin is actively working on that, actually. He’s already pushing on to the next steps.”

The study was supported by a National Science Foundation CAREER grant.

Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold bear would have been worn on a headdress.

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The 2,200-year-old gold bear is a unique find in Kazakhstan.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.

Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan excavated a 2,200-year-old burial mound.

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.

It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

Archaeologists found a surprising number of human bones in the burial mound.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."

After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.

Margherita is a trilingual freelance writer specializing in science and history writing with a particular interest in archaeology, palaeontology, astronomy and human behavior. She earned her BA from Boston College in English literature, ancient history and French, and her journalism MA from L'École Du Journalisme de Nice in International New Media Journalism. In addition to Live Science, her bylines include Smithsonian Magazine, Discovery Magazine, BBC Travel, Atlas Obscura and more.

#6393. What Is a Thought Made Of? Scientists Reveal Why Human Consciousness May Be Beyond the Reach of AI

A familiar song can pull you back decades in an instant, and the chemistry behind that rush of memory may hold clues to what separates human minds from AI.

How does the brain turn a collection of memories into thoughts, emotions, and the experience of being conscious? Scientists have spent decades studying how neurons communicate through electrical and chemical signals, yet the physical processes that allow us to recall experiences, attach feelings to them, and give them meaning remain incompletely understood.

A new scientific review suggests that part of the answer may lie in the complex chemistry surrounding brain cells. Rather than viewing memory primarily as a product of neuronal activity, the researchers propose that interactions among neurons, supporting brain cells, and molecules in their surrounding environment could play a fundamental role in shaping thought and conscious experience.

Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Prof. Chaim Gilon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Department of Chemistry present their theory in Consciousness, Memory, and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective. Building on earlier research into how experiences might be physically stored in the brain, they examine whether the chemistry of memory could help explain the origins of thought and consciousness.

Their proposal also raises a question about artificial intelligence: If human memory and emotion depend on the chemistry of living cells, can computers ever develop consciousness simply by becoming more powerful?

Scientists have long studied how neurons communicate to form and retrieve memories. But Marx and Gilon suggest that important parts of this process may also occur in the molecular environment surrounding brain cells.

Their model, called the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory, involves three interacting components: brain cells, particularly neurons and astrocytes; the molecular material surrounding those cells; and chemicals such as metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

According to the theory, these components could allow the brain to chemically encode and retrieve information. Rather than serving only as a support structure, the environment surrounding brain cells may actively participate in memory storage.

Astrocytes, star-shaped cells that interact closely with neurons, play a central role in the proposed mechanism. The researchers suggest that coordinated activity among these cells, neurons, and surrounding molecules could contribute to how memories are formed and processed.

A familiar song can bring back memories from decades ago, complete with feelings that seemed long forgotten. Such experiences show that remembering involves more than retrieving information.

Marx and Gilon propose that the emotional content of memories may be linked to their chemical encoding. In their model, signaling molecules, including neurotransmitters and gliotransmitters, help connect stored information with the feelings associated with an experience.

The researchers also suggest that retrieving and interpreting these chemically stored memories may contribute to the emergence of thought. In this view, memory is not simply a record of past events but an active process through which the brain assigns meaning to experience.

Computers and brains both store and process information, but the underlying mechanisms differ. While computers rely on electronic hardware, biological memory involves living cells and complex chemical interactions.

Marx and Gilon argue that this distinction could matter for consciousness. AI systems can perform increasingly sophisticated intellectual tasks, but their ability to process information does not establish that they experience thoughts or emotions.

For example, an AI system can identify a familiar song and describe the memories or feelings it might evoke in a person. Whether such a system could actually experience nostalgia is a different question.

The researchers suggest that if consciousness depends partly on the biochemical processes involved in human memory, greater computational power alone may not be sufficient to reproduce it.

The proposed model offers a possible connection between memory, emotion, and thought, but it does not establish how physical processes in the brain produce conscious experience.

The authors acknowledge that consciousness remains poorly understood and do not claim to have demonstrated that AI cannot become conscious.

Instead, their work suggests that investigating the chemical mechanisms of memory could help explain how stored experiences acquire emotional meaning and contribute to thought. Whether those processes are essential for consciousness remains an open question.

Reference: “Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective” by Gerard Marx and Chaim Gilon, 4 August 2026, International Journal of Psychiatry Research. DOI: 10.33425/2641-4317.1251

#6392. The 7 Best Noise-Canceling Headphones Clear Out the World So You Can Listen to What You Love

These cans and earbuds knock out background noise so you can focus or relax.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Noise-canceling headphones were once a niche category, dominated by high-priced over-ear cans. Throughout most of the 2010s, those seeking to drown out ambient noise distractions at work or during travel had to spend upward of $300 to get a pair up to the task. These days, that's no longer the case. The market is jam-packed with quality noise-canceling headphones, including reliable models that start below $100. Having so many options to choose from can rightfully be overwhelming even for tech-savvy shoppers. To help you find the best noise-canceling headphones worth investing in, I spent months testing highly rated options from leading brands and created this buying guide to share my recommendations.

Read more related reviews in our best wireless headphones and best wireless earbuds buying guides.

I’ve been testing consumer tech products, including audio gear, since 2011. Before I began testing, I spent a day sifting through product specs and features to handpick up-to-date products from reputable makers across the price spectrum—from budget to premium.

My testing routine included spending at least a week with each headset on this list. I used it at work, during my daily commutes, and, of course, while traveling domestically and internationally. These scenarios allowed me to properly evaluate the products’ design and ergonomics.

To evaluate the audio performance of the headphones, I streamed a carefully curated Apple Music playlist with tracks in various genres, including live albums. The eclectic music selection helped me experience the ability of the headphones to produce bass, treble, and midrange. I also used the cans to stream podcasts, watch video content, and play video games.

Traveling by plane and working in a large open office gave me perfect scenarios to test the noise-canceling capabilities of all headphones. I paid close attention to how each set performed in this critical area, keeping in mind its form factor and price tag.

Ambient mode for being aware of your surroundings is just as essential and a key component of my testing routine. I also made sure that the headphones performed well during telephone, FaceTime, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom calls.

Regarding battery life, I meticulously observed how frequently I had to charge each headset. Spending days without battery anxiety was a benchmark for excellence in this department.

Lastly, where available, I tinkered with the companion app of every pair of headphones. I looked for tools to customize sound and additional features that help enhance the overall experience.

With all of the above tips in mind, enjoy a more peaceful daily and travel routine by switching to one of the products I vouch for below.

Bose QuietComfort headphones (and earbuds) have been synonymous with best-in-class noise cancellation for years. It stands to reason, then, that the Ultra cans top this product category.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 headphones, which launched in late 2025, offer up to 30 hours of battery life and superior wired playback. The headphones’ ability to tune out ambient noise distractions by generating almost complete silence is commendable and alone worth splurging on. What’s more, their companion app lets you customize its intensity and save the setting for easy access in a specific scenario. Such a level of modularity sets the product apart from its rivals, just as the core feature’s performance does.

On the audio front, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones deliver a balanced sound that’s customizable via an app. Dubbed Bose Immersive Audio, the cans’ ability to deliver multidimensional spatial sound with optional head tracking is superb and, crucially, easy to access. I like that the feature works with any audio content rather than requiring Dolby Atmos-enhanced audio. I successfully used it to make live music albums and videos more lifelike during my testing.

The 24-hour battery life of the QuietComfort Ultra headphones leaves a little to be desired, as competitors, including those in lower price tiers, can last longer between charges.

With an under-$100 sticker before additional and frequent discounts, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 noise-canceling headphones by 1More are a legit impulse buy for such a product without skimping on design, ergonomics, performance, and battery life. The cans are surprisingly sleek and comfy, capable of delivering a high-quality audio experience across the board, as well as long battery life.

The sound quality of the headphones thoroughly exceeded my expectations when I put them through their paces. Tuned by a master audio engineer, the cans treated me to a balanced sound that made me feel like I was using a much pricier set. The tools for customizing the sound via their companion app are just as impressive.

When it comes to noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 is among the best for the money. The headphones did a solid job in tuning out distractions, but couldn’t match the serenity of costlier cans. That’s totally fine considering their agreeable price.

With up to a staggering 65 hours of battery life with noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 leaves rivals that cost several times more in the dust. I could easily spend a week using them without battery anxiety. And believe it or not, you can get up to 100 hours of wireless playback from the 1More headphones by disabling the core functionality.

The Beats Studio Pro headphones are a must-have for owners of multiple Apple devices. Just like AirPods (and other Beats products), the cans will instantly connect to Apple devices that are linked to the same iCloud account. Once I paired them with my iPhone, I could instantly use the cans with an iPad, a MacBook, and a Mac mini, as well as keep tabs on their whereabouts in the Apple Find My app.

In addition to the seamless hardware compatibility mentioned above, the Beats Studio Pro headphones deserve the attention of Apple users for their ability to deliver a superb spatial audio experience. Accessing the functionality on an iPhone or an iPad is as easy as long-pressing the volume control button in the command center.

The Studio Pro headphones’ audio quality and noise cancellation are among the best in their price category. Their sound is balanced, melodic, and versatile, making it suitable for a wide range of music styles. There is no option to customize it via an app, but I didn’t feel like I had to make any changes while using the cans.

Unlike many competitors, the Beats Studio Pro headphones can deliver lossless audio over a direct USB-C link to phone, tablet, or computer. Listening in higher fidelity doesn’t include noise cancellation. Thankfully, I could access the latter via the standard audio jack when I needed to use the entertainment system during a flight.

The Beats headphones integrate well with Android and Chrome OS hardware, too, but I prefer the Apple experience for its superior spatial audio and because I don't need to install a companion app. Consider the recently released AirPods Max 2 over the Beats Studio Pro if you have a bigger budget for Apple-ready headphones. Their audio performance, craftsmanship, and controls are on a much higher level. However, you’ll have to settle for a heavier headset with shorter battery life and spend extra on a suitable protective case and a cable with a standard audio connector.

On-ear headphones have largely taken a back seat to larger over-ear ANC headphones, which offer more passive noise cancellation, and earbuds for their pocketable form factor. Marshall’s Milton ANC headphones offer a now-rare premium on-ear design that gives you the best version of a middle ground between the two, with a lightweight design, great sound quality, and a less ostentatious on-ear fit. With a foldable design and scratch-resistant ear cup covers, the Milton wears really well over the course of a long day on the go.

On the audio front, the Marshall Milton ANC impressed me with crisp, energetic sound that's customizable via a companion app. Its noise cancellation is also stellar, though does not generate the same auditory void as my top over-ear picks.

The headphones’ knob and customizable button controls are a benchmark for excellence and miles ahead of their competitors. The same goes for its 50-hour battery life. (Or 80 hours if you turn the ANC off.)

On-ear headphones are especially niche if ANC is your top priority, but it’s a great everyday carry headphone if your earbuds just aren’t cutting it. If you dig Marshall’s look, but would prefer an over-ear solution, the Monitor III ANC has a similar design and controls, but with a heavier, more deeply isolating form factor.

Reviewed: Marshall Milton ANC Wireless Headphones

The Bowers & Wilkins PX8 S2 wireless headphones are, hands down, my favorite wireless ANC headphones for discerning audiophiles looking for something more detailed than the standard options from Sony, Bose, and Apple.

Like the legendary British audio maker’s (very) expensive floor speakers, these over-ear cans produce pristine, infinitely customizable stereo sound that faithfully generates every detail of whatever you’re listening to.

At a time when wireless headphones generally try to earn attention with digital enhancements like spatial audio, the PX8 S2 impressed me with Their old-school approach to audio fidelity. (Note: B&W has added spatial audio since my review via a firmware update.) Experiencing the headphones’ sound with noise cancellation enabled is like listening to Bowers & Wilkins speakers in your own private space.

For $800, you know every aspect of these headphones has to work incredibly well, and they do. Its craftsmanship and tactility, headlined by genuine leather and metal accents in several colors, are a marvel for folks with extremely discerning taste... And plenty of disposable income.

The Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are all about delivering incredibly powerful bass that’s available and adjustable via a dedicated button on the left cup. The sensory experience is truly remarkable and unlike anything rivals can offer, even though it predictably impacts the overall audio fidelity. The headphones’ noise cancellation is solid, if not on par with pricier sets from leading makers.

I didn’t reach for the Crusher ANC 2 when I felt like streaming classical jazz, but I grinned every time I played my favorite downtempo tracks on the product. Using the cans for playing action-packed games with the bass cranked up was also a ton of fun.

Disabling the thunderous low-end brought me a more “grown-up” sound, customizable via an app. That’s not what I’d recommend the product for, however. This Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 is all about celebrating bass.

The Crusher ANC 2 is also comfy to wear and equipped with convenient button controls. I also like the headphones’ integrated Tile tracker, as well as their sleek design with a contrasting, brightly colored button for activating the Crusher experience. There are tons of color options.

Skullcandy’s Icon ANC wireless headphones are handily the best for exercising on this list. The surprisingly affordable cans have a compact on-ear design, a secure fit, and an IPX4 rating for sweat- and water resistance. These qualities, together with convenient button controls, make the Icon ANC equally suitable for indoor and outdoor workouts.

The default sound of the headphones has an enhanced bass, which helped me stay motivated during my workouts. The Skullcandy app has several presets for customizing the sound, as well as a graphic equalizer to create your own. The noise cancellation worked, but it didn’t stop me in my tracks with its efficiency. That’s hardly a surprise considering the product’s price category.

I found the Skullcandy Icon ANC’s multidirectional control knob to be incredibly convenient during my testing. Their 50-hour battery life with noise cancellation exceeded my expectations, too. I didn’t expect this longevity from a compact pair of wireless headphones.

Skullcandy offers the Icon ANC in several colors. Every set comes bundled with a soft carrying pouch.

Noise cancellation relies on built-in microphones that continuously monitor your surroundings. A dedicated chip processes the sound captured by the microphones before sending its exact aural opposite to your ears via the headphones' audio drivers. This sophisticated technology naturally contributes to the cost of noise-canceling headphones. Translation? The more you spend, the better you'll isolate yourself from your surroundings. Prepare to drop north of $300 if you are looking to achieve (almost) complete silence from your purchase.

High-quality sound is also a must for a great pair of noise-canceling headphones. Support for immersive spatial audio is particularly important for top-shelf headphones. It makes live albums and video content more immersive and the listening experience more lifelike, especially if dynamic head tracking is available. Spatial audio is available on most top-shelf noise-canceling headphones. High-end sets without this functionality make up for it by producing pristine stereo sound, which makes them worth investing in. Speaking of stereo sound, today's best headphones in this space, including budget-friendly models, support lossless audio over wireless and wired connections. If you are using a streaming service that offers lossless audio, keep an eye out for this feature. It will serve you well.

Your next set of headphones should get you at least 20 to 30 hours of wireless playback between power-ups with noise cancellation. That’s the bare minimum for these products, with class-leading sets by Apple, Bose, and Sony delivering battery endurance in this ballpark. That’s enough to get you through a long flight or hectic workday in silence.Remarkably, cheaper cans now have much longer battery life. Some will give you double the endurance of the class-leading options with noise cancellation and a three-digit number of hours without it. Those numbers are remarkable, but trust me, stronger noise cancellation and higher-quality sound are worth the more frequent charging sessions.

A companion app for customizing the sound and the noise cancellation, among other things, is essential for any set of wireless headphones or earbuds today, so look for it while shopping. Apple AirPods and Beats products don’t have an iPhone app. Their settings are easily accessible directly in iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Stefan is an award-winning consumer technology editor with over a decade of experience in reviewing gadgets, particularly smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, desktop and laptop computers across multiple form factors and platforms, as well as accessories for them. He also covers televisions and audio equipment, including headphones, earbuds, wireless speakers, and soundbars. Since joining Hearst in 2015, Stefan has contributed to BestProducts, Popular Mechanics, and numerous other publications. Prior to his current role, he served as the US Editor for GSMArena.com.

#6391. Stanford Scientists Discover 3 Hidden Brain Types in Children With ADHD and Anxiety

Scientists have identified three distinct patterns of brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both, revealing biological differences that traditional diagnoses often overlook.

Brain scans have uncovered three distinct patterns of disrupted brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both conditions. These patterns do not align neatly with conventional diagnoses, suggesting that children with similar symptoms may have different underlying neurological differences. Some patterns were even detectable years before children received a diagnosis.

The findings come from a Stanford Medicine-led study published October 16 in Nature Mental Health. By combining artificial intelligence with thousands of functional MRI (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three brain biotypes associated with different combinations of behavioral, emotional, and attention difficulties.

ADHD and anxiety are among the most common childhood mental health disorders, and their symptoms frequently overlap. Clinicians typically diagnose these conditions using behavioral assessments and symptom checklists, but those categories may not fully capture the neurological differences between children.

“The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine and co-senior author of the study.

“We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic,” Zhang said.

The researchers found that children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both could belong to any of the three biotypes. Although particular brain patterns were more common with certain diagnoses, no biotype corresponded exclusively to a single disorder.

The researchers identified three neurological profiles, each associated with a distinctive combination of symptoms:

Each child belonged to just one biotype (each child was in only one biotype), but the three patterns appeared across all conventional diagnostic categories.

The model also identified two underlying dimensions of brain dysfunction: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction. Each involved different networks of brain regions, with the three biotypes reflecting distinct combinations of these disruptions. The findings suggest that differences in how brain circuits communicate may help explain variations in children’s symptoms.

The researchers drew on the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, a long-term investigation of more than 11,000 U.S. children who entered the project at ages 9 or 10.

Their analysis included 3,508 children initially diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both; 693 children who received one or both diagnoses later; and 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis. The researchers also examined brain scans from 224 children with ADHD or anxiety in the separate Healthy Brain Network study to validate their findings.

An AI model examined functional connectivity, which describes how activity in different brain regions is coordinated. By combining these measurements with diagnostic records and cognitive and behavioral assessments, the researchers identified brain connectivity patterns associated with ADHD and anxiety that differed from those seen in children without either diagnosis.

The researchers also detected the biotypes in initial brain scans from children who had not yet been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety but developed one or both conditions later. This suggests that certain patterns of brain connectivity may emerge before symptoms lead to a clinical diagnosis.

“We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions,” Zhang said. He identified the early appearance of these patterns as one of the study’s most surprising results.

“It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression.”

The findings do not establish that brain scans can reliably predict which individual children will develop ADHD or anxiety. Further research is needed to determine whether the biotypes can serve as clinically useful biomarkers for early identification.

Beyond early detection, the researchers hope the findings could eventually help clinicians select treatments based on a child’s underlying brain activity rather than relying entirely on symptoms.

Current treatment decisions often involve considerable trial and error, particularly when medications do not produce the expected improvement.

“When doctors prescribe a new medication, it can take quite a long time, a couple of weeks or months, to see a response,” Zhang said. “If the first medication doesn’t work, they switch to a different one,” a process that can be costly, slow, and frustrating for families.

Zhang does not expect brain biotypes to replace existing diagnostic methods. Instead, he envisions using them alongside conventional assessments to provide a more detailed picture of each child’s condition.

Future clinical trials could investigate whether particular treatments improve the brain connectivity abnormalities associated with each biotype. Researchers could then examine whether these neurological patterns help predict treatment responses.

“We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time,” Zhang said.

Reference: “Deep learning of brain–behavior dimensions identifies transdiagnostic biotypes in youth with ADHD and anxiety disorders” by Yong Jiao, Xiaoyu Tong, Gregory A. Fonzo, Ian H. Gotlib, Kilian M. Pohl, Theodore D. Satterthwaite, Jing Jiang and Yu Zhang, 16 October 2026, Nature Mental Health. DOI: 10.1038/s44220-026-00740-3

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01MH129694, R01MH136197, R01MH145082, R01MH140425, U24AA021697, R01DA057567, R37MH101495 and R01MH132784), the Eagles Autism Foundation, the Stanford Knight Initiative for Brain Resilience, the Rosenkranz Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Effie and Wofford Cain Foundation.

Archaeologists have discovered the shoe of the first governor of the Danish West Indies, recovered from a 17th-century ship that was wrecked after one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark’s history.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Maritime archaeologists investigating a 17th-century shipwreck off the coast of Sweden have discovered a fancy shoe and two metal rings used as currency in the transatlantic slave trade. The items were lost during a mutiny on a slave ship in 1683, during which the governor of the Danish West Indies was thrown overboard.

The Danish frigate Havmanden (which translates to "Merman") was en route to St. Thomas, a Caribbean island that is now part of the U.S. Virgin Islands, with convicts and indentured servants aboard destined for work on the island with the Danish West India Company. The plan for the Havmanden, after dropping off the new colonists, was to sail to West Africa to buy enslaved Africans. But due to a shortage of food and water, several crewmembers and convicts aboard seized control of the ship near the Azores in the North Atlantic and began sailing it back to Copenhagen.

The mutineers shot the ship's captain and threw other officers ‪—‬ including Jørgen Iversen Dyppel, the first governor of the Danish West Indies ‪—‬ overboard in the English Channel. After the ship ran aground, the mutineers were tried for their crimes in Copenhagen and sentenced to death.

The story of the Havmanden is one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark's history, according to a Nov. 11 translated statement from the National Museum of Denmark. But now, underwater archaeologists are learning more about the fateful voyage from the wreck, which lies on the seabed just east of Gothenburg, Sweden.

Archaeological divers discovered the rear half of a man's "unusually fine" shoe in the wreckage, according to the statement.

"I see a great many shoes from shipwrecks, but I have never before seen a shoe of such high quality," Vivi Lena Andersen, director of the Rudersdal Museums in Denmark, said in the statement.

The sole has a high level of craftsmanship, Andersen said, which can be seen in the minuscule holes perforating the edge of the shoe. The regularity of the holes would have required tools and expertise that only the most skilled shoemakers had at the time. It was "undoubtedly an expensive and exclusive shoe that only the elite could afford to buy," Andersen said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Because the shoe was likely owned by an upper-class individual, experts think it could have belonged to Iversen, the Danish West Indies governor who was thrown overboard.

"The shoe testifies not only to Jørgen Iversen Dyppel's life and dramatic death, but also provides a personal point of entry into the larger story of the establishment of the Danish colonies in the West Indies and the widespread slave trade Denmark was a part of," Andreas Kallmeyer Bloch, a maritime archaeologist at the National Museum of Denmark's Center for Maritime and Underwater Cultural Heritage, said in the statement.

Additional clues to the Danish slave trade on board the Havmanden included two manillas, ring-shaped pieces of metal that were used as currency in West Africa. European merchants cast manillas from copper, brass or iron and traded them for enslaved people in West Africa, particularly along the coast of modern-day Nigeria. But manillas are rarely found in Scandinavia, according to the statement.

"The manillas add another layer to Havmanden's story and underscore the connection to the slave trade, which was a central part of Denmark's colonial activities in both the West Indies and on the west coast of Africa," Kallmeyer Bloch said.

Denmark continued to engage in the transatlantic slave trade for more than a century after the Havmanden sank. Although King Christian VII of Denmark-Norway banned the trade in 1792, slavery continued in the Danish West Indies until 1848, when hundreds of enslaved people revolted and were finally granted their freedom.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6389. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#6388. Scientists Find That Mice, Not Deer, Hold a Major Clue to Lyme Disease Risk

A 35-year study reveals that mice, acorns, and unexpected environmental forces hold surprising clues to predicting Lyme disease risk. A remarkable 35-year study is challenging long-held assumptions about Lyme disease, revealing that mice, acorns, and even extreme weather influence tick populations in unexpected ways. One of the biggest surprises is that deer, often associated with the spread of Lyme disease, may be less important in predicting the numbers of dangerous ticks than researchers once believed.

Diseases transmitted by ticks are becoming increasingly common across the United States. Lyme disease is the most frequently reported, with nearly 500,000 people diagnosed annually. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through bites from infected blacklegged ticks. Antibiotics can successfully treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may spread to the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have investigated the complicated relationships among oak trees, acorns, rodents, predators, ticks, and climate. Their goal has been to understand how these interconnected factors influence the risk of Lyme disease in humans.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences highlights nine particularly unexpected discoveries from this decades-long research effort. Several findings challenge conventional thinking about how tick populations grow and what determines the likelihood of disease transmission.

“On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the unusually extensive dataset has been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from random fluctuations and misleading correlations. Relationships that seem convincing over a few years can look very different when examined across several decades.

“Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare,” said LaDeau. “This research has followed an ecological community — including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms — examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study.”

When scientists first identified Lyme disease in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely factor in the disease’s spread. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying large numbers of adult ticks, suggesting that deer populations might strongly influence how many ticks would emerge in subsequent seasons.

Deer do not directly transmit the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks. However, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks, allowing those ticks to reproduce. Researchers therefore suspected that larger deer populations would support more egg-laying females and ultimately produce more young ticks.

Decades of field observations have complicated that theory. At the Cary Institute’s 2,000-acre forested research site in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant relationship between deer abundance and the number of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks and represent the life stage most likely to transmit Lyme disease to humans.

“We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data,” said Ostfeld, “but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing.”

Although deer numbers did not reliably predict nymph populations, mouse numbers told a different story.

The researchers discovered that years with abundant mice were followed by an approximately 40% increase in nymphal ticks the next year. This relationship makes white-footed mice particularly important to understanding changes in tick populations.

These small rodents provide an excellent food source for blacklegged tick larvae. They are also highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to the young ticks feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can carry the bacteria into their next developmental stage. When they feed again as nymphs, they can transmit the infection to humans.

One of the study’s most striking discoveries involves something seemingly unrelated to human disease: acorns.

Oak trees occasionally produce unusually large quantities of acorns in a synchronized event known as acorn masting. The sudden abundance of food benefits mice, allowing their populations to increase during the following year.

That population boom then provides more feeding opportunities for young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly large acorn harvest can reliably predict increased numbers of nymphal ticks two years later.

This creates a remarkable ecological chain reaction in which events beginning in the forest canopy can influence tick populations years afterward.

The relationship between mice and Lyme disease produced another unexpected finding.

Because mice are so effective at transmitting B. burgdorferi, the scientists initially assumed that years with more mice would also have a higher percentage of infected nymphal ticks. Early observations appeared to support that prediction.

However, the connection gradually disappeared as the research team accumulated more years of data.

“It kept me up at night,” said Ostfeld, “because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.”

Further investigation pointed toward a more complicated explanation involving other animals that provide blood meals for ticks.

When mouse populations increase, populations of other potential hosts, including squirrels, skunks, and opossums, may also rise. Most of these animals are much less effective at transmitting the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks.

Consequently, a greater share of ticks feeding on these alternative hosts can reduce the overall percentage of infected nymphs, even when mice are plentiful.

“So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts,” explained Ostfeld. “It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case.”

The findings demonstrate why predicting the total number of ticks is different from predicting how many of those ticks carry Lyme disease.

Another surprise emerged when the researchers compared laboratory experiments with conditions in the wild.

Previous laboratory studies had suggested that extreme heat and severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that the insects were far more resilient than expected.

The researchers suspect that ticks escape dangerous temperatures by moving deeper into the soil or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less extreme.

However, temperature still appears to influence tick populations in important ways. The team found that years with generally warmer conditions tended to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual.

This creates an intriguing contradiction. Warmer years typically benefit mice, which should help support larger tick populations, yet the researchers have not observed a corresponding overall increase in nymphs.

Understanding how these opposing effects interact remains an important focus of the ongoing research.

Together, the discoveries suggest that Lyme disease risk is shaped by a complicated network of ecological relationships, but one that contains patterns scientists can use to make predictions.

The strong connection between mouse abundance and future tick numbers could help public health officials anticipate periods of elevated risk. Likewise, recognizing that deer abundance is not a reliable predictor of nymph populations at the study site, and that severe winter weather may not substantially reduce tick numbers, could improve disease prevention strategies.

Important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will influence the relationships among ticks, rodents, oak trees, and other wildlife.

“You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far,” said Ostfeld. “We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it’s very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production.”

Since the monitoring program began in 1991, its research site in Dutchess County has undergone numerous environmental changes, including shifting climate conditions, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species.

The scientists intend to continue tracking how ticks and the animals they depend on respond to these changes. By extending an already exceptional research record, they hope to uncover more of the hidden ecological patterns that could help predict Lyme disease risk and protect human health in the years ahead.

Reference: “The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis” by Richard S. Ostfeld, Shannon L. LaDeau, Kelly Oggenfuss, Charles D. Canham, Michael Fargione, Raymond J. Winchcombe and Felicia Keesing, 17 August 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2610907123

#6386. This Dietary Supplement Could Have Potential Brain Benefits, Study Finds

A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising new questions about its potential benefits.

When the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients. For people with obesity, changes in blood vessel function can affect circulation, raising questions about how well the brain responds to these demands. A new clinical trial suggests a dietary supplement could help increase blood flow during mental activity, although researchers have yet to show that it improves memory.

Researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts. The amount people naturally produce varies, and existing research suggests that production declines with age and increasing body mass index. Urolithin A is also available as a dietary supplement.

In the randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA Network Open, 50 adults with obesity, ages 40 to 64, received either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A daily or a placebo for four weeks.

Participants taking the supplement showed a greater increase in blood flow to the brain while completing a challenging memory task. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area involved in holding and using information over short periods. However, researchers found no significant improvements in blood vessel function in the arm or performance on memory tests.

“The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity,” said first author Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.”

According to the researchers, this is the first human study to report an effect of urolithin A on blood vessel function in the brain. The supplement was well-tolerated, although the trial involved relatively few participants at a single research site. Longer studies with larger groups will be needed to determine whether the changes in blood flow lead to lasting health benefits.

“These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain,” said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. “Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.”

The researchers ultimately hope to find ways to help people maintain their cognitive health as they age.

“The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline,” Langley said. “We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.”

Reference: “Urolithin A and Endothelial and Cerebrovascular Function in Middle-Aged Adults With Obesity: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley, Rafal Gulej, Zalan Kaposzta, Zsofia Szarvas, Ali Shahriari, Henry Kinnard, Bryan Ticer, Camila B. Pinto, Peter Mukli, Mihaly Muranyi, Cheryl Adams, Jeng Kong, Leah Anderson, Stefano Tarantini, Yan Daniel Zhao, Norman G. Hord and Andriy Yabluchanskiy, 9 October 2026, JAMA Network Open. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38047

Research reported in this publication was supported by the American Heart Association (grant No. 24DIVSUP1282484 awarded to Dr da Costa Pinaffi-Langley) and the Reynolds Foundation.

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.
