#6279. Another bill to release Epstein files headed to House floor

Massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

As Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie said his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he said, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie said. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor."

A recent satellite photo captured an underwater cloud of fish sperm, or milt, appearing to glow green during a Pacific herring spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along the coast of Canada's Vancouver Island.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada [48.95586624, -125.42994277]

What's in the photo? A green cloud of milt (fish sperm) and eggs during a Pacific herring spawning event

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This surprising satellite snap shows a giant underwater plume of fish sperm that seems to glow green beneath the waves. The colorful cloud appeared during a spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along Canada's western coastline.

The striking sight was spotted in Barkley Sound, along a section of the southern coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, roughly 45 miles (70 kilometers) north of the U.S. border. The bright-green cloud is the most concentrated between Salmon Beach — the triangular town in the center of the image — and the smaller Forbes Island, which is also "glowing" along its northern coast.

The green cloud is around 4 miles (7 km) from end to end and is made of milt — a fluid containing sperm made by fish, mollusks and other aquatic animals — that was released during a Pacific herring (Clupea pallasii) spawning event. Like many other fish species, Pacific herring reproduce by congregating in large groups. The females lay eggs, which stick to kelp, sea grasses and rocky surfaces, before the males release their milt, which disperses over the area and fertilizes the eggs.

Pacific herring, which grow to around 10 inches (25 centimeters) long, often congregate in this spot off Vancouver Island in late winter or early spring, gathering for several weeks before releasing their gametes, or sex cells, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

"The herring spawn is a really fabulous time to be out here," local resident Ryan Cutler, who used a drone to capture close-up photos of this year's spawning event (see below), told CBC News. "It's a really, really spectacular time to be around."

The cloud of milt arguably looks even more imposing up close, as you can see in this drone photo from resident Ryan Cutler, who described the spawning event as "fabulous" and "spectacular."

Spawning events can last anywhere between a few hours and several days, and scientists are increasingly turning to satellite images to help monitor these occurrences, according to the Earth Observatory. In this case, the milt cloud was visible for around 48 hours.

While the milky substance appears a striking green in these images, it is actually white. It appears green only because it is closer to the surface than the surrounding seafloor, meaning that less reflected light is absorbed by the water. This is also why shallow patches of water often appear turquoise when viewed from above.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The coastline alongside Salmon Beach is perfect for herring to spawn because it strikes the perfect balance between a number of important factors. "Herrings prefer spawning locations that are more protected, have rocky substrate, and allow them to select areas with reduced salinity," Jessica Moffatt, a biologist with Vancouver Island's Island Marine Aquatic Working Group, told the Earth Observatory. "Barkley Sound hits the 'sweet spot' in many of these regards."

The Pacific herring is an important species in this region; it is a primary food source for Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), which give Salmon Beach its name. The herring are also hunted by local First Nation groups, according to CBC News.

During the spawning events, a wide range of other predatory marine life — including large fish, whales and sea lions — are drawn to the area to feast on the herring, according to the Earth Observatory. And on land, eagles, wolves and bears are more likely to appear during the mass reproduction event.

The milt appears green from above due to how wavelengths are absorbed by water as light reflects off the the white substance.

Coincidentally, this exact patch of ocean was the site of one of the weirdest oceanographic events ever seen. In 2020, around 4 miles (7 km) off the coast of Ucluelet (located just along the coastline to the left in the photo), scientists detected a rogue wave that appeared in the open ocean seemingly from nowhere. The massive wave reached the height of a four-story building, making it the most extreme version of this phenomenon ever seen.

Farther offshore, around 150 miles (240 km) south of Vancouver Island, researchers also detected a surprise swarm of more than 2,000 underwater earthquakes in a single day in March 2024, hinting that a section of the seafloor was ripping apart.

A recent satellite photo captured a series of clouds sculpted by von Kármán vortices from a volcano on South Korea's Jeju Island. A giant multicolor plume, ejected by China's Yangtze River, is also visible in the image.

A recent satellite photo captured a gleaming halo of phytoplankton encircling the remote Chatham Islands. The stunning sight is the result of a hidden underwater structure, which has also helped kill hundreds of cetaceans.

A recent satellite photo captured a stunning scene of sediment swirling across the West Florida Shelf after an extreme cold snap that covered large parts of the eastern U.S. in snow.

#6275. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI worms could spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting smart devices

Common forms of cyberattack include viruses and worms. Researchers recently added new styles of attack to the twisted menagerie: worms that act more like octopuses or slime molds.

VICTOR HABBICK VISIONS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.)

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”

Anthropic. AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter. 2026.

O. Çetin et al. Cleaning up the internet of evil things: real-world evidence on ISP and consumer efforts to remove Mirai. Network and Distributed Systems Security (NDSS) Symposium, San Diego, 2019.

In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear," author and environmental historian Peter S. Alagona looks at the models used to develop the U.S. grizzly bear recovery program, and how California could make an ideal home for a new population.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are.

But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet" (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out.

Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. They assume that conservation efforts should focus on the best remaining grizzly habitats, and that we can best understand those habitats by studying bears in the places where they still live.

The result has, indeed, been a far better understanding of grizzly habitat use. But this approach has also produced a circular logic with a structural bias toward the status quo. In most grizzly habitat models, past realities and future possibilities fade. With each new study, it seems more and more like the only possible places for grizzlies are the exact kinds of places where they currently live.

The six recovery areas identified in the 1993 Recovery Plan were all places where grizzlies still lived or had recently lived when they were listed as threatened in 1975. The plan argued that these areas "had the potential to provide adequate space and habitat to maintain the grizzly bear as a viable and self-sustaining species." But it also acknowledged the risks and uncertainties facing the bears, and it pledged to assess other areas in their historical range.

This process was expected to take five years. Twenty-eight years later, in 2019, the FWS settled a federal lawsuit in which it agreed to finally conduct this long-delayed analysis. It built a simple model based mainly on secure habitat, and then applied it to both the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and the Sierra Nevada of California. Other potential recovery areas — such as the North Rim of the Grand Canyon in Arizona, the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico, and the Northwest Forest of Northern California — were, for unexplained reasons, not included.

The current grizzly bear recovery zones with the proposed boundaries.

The model did its job. According to the FWS, neither the San Juans nor the Sierra Nevada contained enough secure habitat to support a viable grizzly population. Instead of subjecting the study to peer review, the FWS published it in an appendix on page 286 of a species status report. Having pioneered the idea of secure habitat, David Mattson now set out to explain why the FWS was abusing it. In his view, the service's models focused on artificially small areas, failed to consider several key factors described in the scientific literature, and neglected to conduct essential supporting analyses to explain its conclusions.

The FWS had dragged its heels for almost three decades, and then, after pledging in court to conduct a good-faith analysis, produced a study that seemed designed to reach a predetermined result: The only places capable of supporting grizzlies were the places where the FWS was already trying to recover them. When Mattson and his colleague Troy Merrill ran a more detailed model for the southwestern states, they found that Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah contained seven potential recovery areas with more than 45,000 square kilometers of suitable habitat that could probably support more than 1,000 bears.

For more than a century, the prevailing narrative in California has been that the grizzly's extinction there was inevitable and its recovery is impossible. But Mattson's results for the southwest, combined with California's unique geography, cast doubt on this story.

California is home to nearly 40 million people, and it has more miles of roads than any state except Texas. But its population is extraordinarily concentrated. California is the most urban state, with 95% of its residents packed into cities and 75% living on only around 2% of its land area. Much of California has a human population density lower than that of the Northern Rockies. Unlike in the Northern Rockies, the majority of California's farms are concentrated in broad valleys dozens of miles from core wilderness habitats.

Kings Canyon National Park in California has been identified as one of the locations where grizzlies could thrive.

Outside urban and agricultural areas, California has more protected land than any state except Alaska, including the largest areas of potential grizzly habitat outside the six current recovery zones. Some of these protected areas are in desert ecosystems not suitable for grizzly bears, but others are in mountain ecosystems with potential grizzly habitat.

California's national parks and wilderness areas sometimes strain under heavy visitation, but the numbers paint a complex picture. Consider the southern High Sierra. In 2024, Sequoia Kings Canyon National Park, which is around 865,000 acres and 97% wilderness, topped 2 million visitors for the first time, whereas Yellowstone, which is around 2.2 million acres and 90% wilderness, received almost 5 million visitors, meaning that both parks had about 2.3 visitors per acre. Yellowstone has more than double the total land area in wilderness, but both parks border large U.S. Forest Service wilderness areas and other public lands, and the High Sierra has fewer roads cutting across its protected areas.

In 2024, I coauthored a study, almost eight years in the making, looking at potential grizzly habitat in California. This project, led by Alex McInturff from the University of Washington, ran four computer models, and then compared them to assess the results each produced. One of these models focused on historical sightings of grizzlies in California, two used approaches developed in other regions where brown bears currently live, and one looked at the habitat use preferences of one of California's other large carnivores, the puma.

The Grizzly Bear Recovery Program was created in the 1970s to restore populations to self-sustaining levels.

Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. None of them fully account for the distribution or abundance of food on the landscape or for possible conflicts with people. Together, however, they provide a first assessment of the amount, quality, and locations of potential grizzly habitats. Amazingly, about a third of California appeared as suitable habitat in all four models.

The biggest areas of high-quality habitat were in the southern Sierra Nevada, around Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, where some of the last California grizzly sightings occurred in the 1920s. The Northwest Forest, along the Pacific Coast near the Oregon border, also scored highly owing to its low human population density and rich forest habitats. The Transverse Ranges, in the state's southwestern corner, scored highly because of their rich chaparral habitats and density of historical sightings, but ranked somewhat lower than the other two because more people live, work, and grow crops, including extensive vineyards and avocado orchards, around its borders.

These results made intuitive sense, given the state's robust historical grizzly population, large areas of protected habitat, and healthy black bear populations. But they represented a departure from the conventional wisdom that dominated the circular logic of most habitat models. For the first time, it was clear how much potential habitat could be available in California for a grizzly recovery. But our approach still clung to the conservative assumption that the grizzly is a wilderness species. We had shown, with some important caveats, that California probably had enough wilderness to support one or more viable grizzly populations.

What we hadn't shown was whether Californians were willing to coexist with grizzlies that might, someday, wander outside the state's wilderness boundaries.

From the book START WITH A BEAR: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet, by Peter S. Alagona. Copyright © 2026 by Peter S. Alagona. Published by HarperOne, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Excerpted by permission.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

A century ago, prevailing wisdom cast large carnivores as adversaries—pests and threats to be removed for human safety and prosperity. In North America, among the most targeted of these animals were brown bears, or grizzlies, whose population decimation has made them emblematic of this fear-driven approach to wildlife management.

In California, where they once roamed the land in the tens of thousands, grizzlys have not been seen in more than 100 years. Modern conservation has evolved, yet it often remains rooted in a separation from nature, a systemic opposition that keeps the wild at arm's length.

In Start with a Bear, historian, ecologist, and bear expert Peter Alagona suggests we must reimagine the very heart of conservation, inviting a new framework for sustainable, reciprocal relations with the wild creatures that remain.

Peter S. Alagona is an environmental historian, conservation scientist, and nature-culture geographer. His work explores what happens when people share space and resources (their habitats) with other species: how we interact with non-human creatures, how we make sense of these interactions, why we fight so much about them, what we can learn from them, and how we might use these lessons to foster a more just, peaceful, humane, and sustainable society. He is a professor of environmental studies at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is the author of "After the Grizzly" and "The Accidental Ecosystem."

#6273. I Tested SwitchBot’s Tiny Robot Vacuum, and It Reaches Under Couches Where Bigger Bots Can’t

It stands just 3.6 inches tall, picks up pet hair and cat litter, and docks in a station that’s nice enough to leave out.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

I’ve had a SwitchBot robot vac running laps around my home’s lower level for more than a year, so I figured the K11+ Pro wouldn’t hold many surprises. The robot itself is the same compact cleaner I already know from the SwitchBot K10+ Pro Combo, minus the handheld attachments that come with the Combo. Then I unpacked the docking station.

It takes up less floor space than a sheet of printer paper, has a creamy finish with a faux wood top, and looks more like home decor than a cleaning appliance. It’s the perfect way to upgrade the form and function of our guest suite—adding a cute cleaning tool without taking up too much space or making the room feel like a utility closet.

SwitchBot calls the K11+ Pro the world’s smallest robot vacuum, and that diminutive size is the whole appeal. Most robot vacuums stop at the edge of the couch or bed. This one disappears underneath furniture and comes back out with the pet hair, lint, and stray cat litter that I can rarely reach with an upright vacuum or cordless stick vac.

After weeks of frequent cleaning, I’ve come to appreciate this little robot for exactly what it is. It’s not a do-everything flagship, and it doesn’t try to be one. It’s one of the easiest robot vacuums to live with—and its price makes it even easier to like.

I ran the K11+ Pro on hardwood, laminate, tile, and low-pile carpeting, and I sent it under every sofa, bed, and dresser it could fit under. My house supplies plenty of test material, including pet hair, tracked cat litter, crumbs, and lint.

I tested the mapping, no-go zones, mopping pads, and voice prompts, and I watched how it maneuvered around pet toys, shoes, blankets, cords, and my weird little cat who likes to get in the way of every robot vacuum. Since I’ve used the K10+ Pro for more than a year, I also had a long-term reference point for how this robot holds up day to day.

At 3.6 inches tall and just under 10 inches wide, the K11+ Pro fits under furniture that blocks most other cleaning robots. It slides beneath my couch and beds without getting wedged, and it cleans hidden zones just as well as the open floor.

Corners usually give round robots trouble, but SwitchBot’s Anti-Tangle Twin Side Brush helps solve this problem. The brush extends to sweep debris out of corners and along walls, so the K11+ Pro gets closer to full edge-to-edge coverage than I expected from a robot this size.

The smaller footprint pays off in another way, too. The robot weighs about 5 pounds, so I can carry it to another room, set it down, and let it work. That makes it handy for a single room, a home office, or a spot that needs a quick cleanup.

With up to 150 minutes of runtime, it can handle my home’s entire lower level before heading back to the dock. When I set it to do just our guest suite, it’s back on the charger long before it runs low on battery.

I didn’t expect a whole lot of cleaning power from a robot this compact, but 12,000 Pa of suction gives the K11+ Pro more pull than its size suggests. I watched it collect pet hair, lint, cat litter, and crumbs from hard floors and the surface of low-pile carpet without leaving trails behind. It’s a solid fit for pet-friendly homes that mostly have hard floors and area rugs.

The rubber roller brush resists tangles. I never had to cut hair off the roller itself, though hair can build up at the ends of the brush. SwitchBot includes a combination cleaning and hair-cutting tool, which handles that in a few seconds.

Thicker carpet is a different story. Like every robot vacuum I’ve tested, the K11+ Pro lifts debris from the top of the carpet but doesn’t reach down to the pad. For deep carpet cleaning, I still rely on a full-size machine like the Dyson Ball Animal 3, since upright and canister vacuums reach deeper into thicker piles.

The K11+ Pro’s docking station is where this model separates itself from the K10+ Pro. It takes up even less room, and the extra-large 4-liter dust bag fills the whole upper cabinet.

SwitchBot says a bag can last up to 90 days, and based on how slowly mine has filled, I believe it. Lifting off the top to check the bag takes a second, and the dock comes with a bag preloaded, so I had it running within minutes of unboxing.

The one catch here is noise. The robot runs at a comfortable volume while it cleans, but the self-emptying cycle gets loud for such a small machine. It lasts only a few seconds, though, and I just schedule runs for times when I don’t need a quiet house.

The K11+ Pro uses LDS LiDAR to map rooms and plan efficient cleaning routes, and side sensors help it steer around chair and table legs. Drop sensors keep it away from stairs, and it climbs thresholds up to 1.7 cm, which includes every transition strip in my house.

I named rooms on the map and set no-go zones in a few minutes. It steered around pet toys, blankets, and shoes, and kept cleaning even while one of my cats stalked it from room to room. It will swallow cords, though, so check under and behind furniture before a run.

It also lacks the headlight many costlier robots use to spot obstacles and stay visible in dark rooms. LiDAR units don't need light to map or run, so I didn’t notice any trouble with navigation, but it’s worth knowing if having a lighted vacuum matters to you.

The K11+ Pro comes with premoistened mopping pads you attach to the bottom of the unit by hand, and they work for light cleanup on hard floors. But think of it as making passes with a Swiffer rather than a powerful scrub. The pads pick up dust and light spills, and the no-go zones come in handy for keeping the damp pad off rugs and carpet.

If you need deep mopping, you’ll want a different tool for the job. A wet-dry vacuum like the Dreame H15 Pro Heat or G10 Pro tackles sticky spills and dried-on messes, and a robot with a self-cleaning roller mop, such as the Eufy Omni E35, handles hands-off scrubbing.

Setup was a breeze. I just followed the quick-start guide: turn on the switch under the top cover, open the app, and connect it to WiFi. I already had the SwitchBot app loaded on my phone, and it connected right away.

I’ve always found the SwitchBot app easy to use. Starting a full cleaning run, picking a single room to tackle, or drawing a no-go zone takes a couple of taps. The robot also talks, announcing what it’s doing and when it needs something, which saves me from checking the app.

If you already run a smart home, it’ll fit right in. The K11+ Pro works with Alexa, Google Home, Apple Home, and Home Assistant without an extra hub.

I love the K11+ Pro, and that comes down to expectations. It’s not a full-size robot vacuum and mop with every bell and whistle. If you want a robot that scrubs floors and washes its own mop, a model like the Eureka J15 Pro Ultra fits that role. The K11+ Pro does something different. It squeezes into tight spaces, cleans under and around furniture, and keeps hard floors and low-pile rugs tidy with very little help from me.

While it’s not the top choice as the main vacuum in a larger home, it’s perfect for apartments, smaller homes, individual rooms, and anyone who wants a dependable robot vacuum for pet hair on hard floors. Pair it with a lightweight stick like the Levoit Aero or another cordless stick vacuum for quick spot cleanups, and you’ve got most of your floors covered.

#6272. Nov. 17, 1966: A phenomenal Leonid meteor storm

On Nov. 17, 1966, the Leonids put on one of the greatest meteor shows in recorded history, during which eyewitnesses reported a sky that seemed to “rain shooting stars.” Observers in North America witnessed a peak of thousands of meteors per minute; Kitt Peak National Observatory reported 40 meteors per second. This peak occurred around 12:00 Universal Time, and lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes. As the requisite rate of 1,000 meteors per hour was not just met but superseded dozens of times over, the event was firmly classified as a true meteor storm.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6271. Rand Paul chooses ranking member slot at Senate HELP

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he plans to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

The move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul said in a press release that he plans to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote

Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he said, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”

But he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”

Lankford said he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”

#6270. The 8 Best Lawn Sweepers Make Clearing Leaves a Breeze

Whether you attach one to your lawn mower or buy a dedicated push-behind model, using a lawn sweeper makes it easy to keep your lawn pristine.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For many of us, the pretty early days of colorful autumn trees have passed, and now we’re dealing with a deluge of leaves covering the ground. During my years in grounds maintenance, much of it landscaping, fall cleanup meant long days with a rake and a blower, then bagging everything we'd piled up. A lawn sweeper thankfully takes most of the bending out of that job and is much more efficient.

With this rake on wheels, it’s the device doing all the work. As it rolls, a gear in each wheel spins a shaft of brushes several times faster than the wheels turn, and the brushes flick leaves, grass clippings, and pine needles back into a fabric hopper—the collection bag stretched over a frame. There's no engine and no cord.

The range of lawn sweepers varies from 26-inch push sweepers you use like a lawn mower, suitable for a small lawn or a patio, to tow-behinds, some of them 54 inches wide, that are pulled with lawn tractors or zero-turn mowers. To find the right one for you, look at how fast a lawn sweeper’s brushes spin at a safe ground speed (the pace you drive or walk), how far the brushes adjust into the grass, and whether the hitch holds the machine level.

Here are our top recommendations spanning various categories and use cases.

With decades of experience testing and researching lawn care equipment, our Popular Mechanics test team compiled the following recommendations based on brands we know and trust. Lawn sweepers are typically suited for large properties, with the majority of our selections in this guide being the type of models you tow behind a lawn tractor.

The recommendations here are capable of clearing large amounts of grass clippings and leaves from lawns that span a half-acre or more. For quarter-acre yards, we generally recommend a leaf blower to clear leaves and a mower with a bagging attachment to collect grass clippings. That said, we still include two lawn sweeping options for smaller yards.

Adding expertise to this article is freelance writer James Fitzgerald, who started as a ranch hand, then apprenticed as a carpenter, and spent several years in residential construction. Fitzgerald followed that with time as a production tree climber and aerial lift operator, then transitioned into facilities and grounds maintenance across multiple residential and commercial properties. All of these efforts involved a great deal of landscaping. His byline has appeared in Family Handyman, Bob Vila, The Spruce, This Old House, and Forbes Home.

For this most recent update, Fitzgerald reviewed manufacturers' specifications, owners' manuals and parts lists, and consumer reviews. For tow-behinds, he gave preference to a published brush-to-wheel ratio (written like 5:1, for five turns of the brushes to each turn of the wheels) and speed limit. Those with a hitch that adjusts to the height of a tractor's hitch plate (the flat bar at the back of the tractor with a hole for the pin) were also given preference. For push sweepers, capacity, weight, and price mattered more.

If you’ve got a lawn tractor and more yard than you want to rake, this is the sweeper that is best. It's one of the pricier picks, but what more money buys you is time. Its brackets assemble for hitch plates (the flat bar at the back of the tractor with a hole for the pin) 7 to 9, 9 to 11, or 11 to 13 inches off the ground, so it rides level whether your hitch sits low or high. The hitch can be offset so that it runs to one side of the tractor, enabling you to pick up the clippings right out of your discharge chute. Picking up already-mowed leaves theoretically lets the collection hopper fit more debris, saving you further time as you don’t have to empty as often.

Its 5.6:1 gearing spins the brushes about 470 times a minute at a 3 mph cruise, fast enough to throw debris to the back of the 28-cubic-foot hopper.

It dumps with a handle you work from the seat, which is better than a rope for the leverage on a full load of wet grass. Empty it more often when the grass is wet, since a heavy load can bend the hopper's support tubes.

At 72.7 pounds, the Yard Commander's 42-inch sweeper is the lightest of the tow-behind options in this guide. Its universal hitch attaches quickly to most lawn tractors and ATVs but not to zero-turn mowers.

Four 10-inch nylon brushes sweep into a 17.79-cubic-foot hopper, which holds a little over three lawn bags' worth and empties with the pull of a string. The corrosion-resistant steel construction delivers stability and ensures use season after season. Yard Commander doesn't publish a gear ratio or a top speed.

This mid-size lawn sweeper behind a tractor is worth a look. Its 42-inch path makes it manageable to steer easily around beds and trees, and the 22-cubic-foot hopper, about four lawn bags' worth, empties with a rope from the seat. Five hitch positions let you choose the one that leaves the hitch tubes (the bars running from the hitch to the sweeper) roughly level with the ground.

Its four spiral brushes twist along the shaft, so part of each always touches the grass and it doesn't bounce and chatter over uneven ground the way straight brushes can. Sealed bearings (ones that come greased and closed) keep dirt and grass dust out of the brush shaft, so it keeps turning freely.

I like fiberglass-reinforced nylon wheels on a machine that lives outdoors, since the glass fiber stiffens them against knocks and a solid wheel can't go flat.

Ohio Steel doesn't publish a wheel size, but a retailer lists 11-inch wheels, and smaller wheels turn more often. At a 3-mph cruise, that puts its 4.5:1 gearing at about 410 brush turns a minute, so its lower ratio costs it less than the number suggests.

Width saves laps on a big lawn, and Brinly's 54-inch sweeper has both the widest path and the largest hopper in this guide, at 54 inches and 30 cubic feet. Brinly says its six Double-Helix brushes (brush strips that twist in a spiral around the shaft) pick up continuously, even through turns. Brinly lists no brush speed, but its 12-inch wheels and 5:1 gearing put it at about 420 turns a minute at a 3 mph cruise, or 560 at the 4-mph cap. A 10-position lock arm sets brush height from about 1/4 inch to 3-1/4 inches, high for deep leaves and low for clippings.

Its clevis (the U-shaped fitting at the front of the hitch that pins to your tractor) mounts two ways, for hitch plates 7 to 10 inches off the ground or 11 to 14, so it rides level on a low hitch or a high one. At nearly 62 inches across, it needs a wide gate and shed door.

Set aside a few hours for assembly. The vinyl hopper is a tight fit, so work it onto the frame a section at a time. With acres to clear and a tractor that fits its hitch, this is the one I'd want. It's the most expensive sweeper in this guide, but the width and the hopper are what the extra money will buy you.

For a lawn that doesn't justify a tractor, Agri-Fab's 26-inch push sweeper is the one I suggest. Its hopper holds 6.2 cubic feet, a little more than one lawn bag, and that’s a lot for a machine this size. Its four brushes are geared at 5:1.

Small wheels help here. Its 9.8-inch wheels turn more often than a tow-behind's, so at a brisk 3-mph walk the brushes spin about 515 times a minute, and they slow down when you do. Brush height adjusts by sliding a tube and locking it with a knob.

At 26 pounds, it's light enough to hang on a garage wall, and the hopper frame comes off if you'd rather store it flat. Upkeep is a few drops of light oil on the brush-shaft bearings twice a year, plus cleaning and lightly greasing the wheel gears every two years.

While it's simple to put together, the plastic body flexes, so be prepared that it pushes hard with the brushes low and needs a flat lawn to pick up well. On a small, level lawn, it's the push sweeper to get.

Scotts' 26-inch push sweeper is the lightest machine recommended here, and it's sized for small jobs like a townhouse lawn, patio, or a driveway after a windy night. Its hopper holds 3.6 bushels, about 4.5 cubic feet, or a little less than one lawn bag, which is the smallest hopper in this guide. The whole sweeper weighs under 22 pounds. The hopper unhooks from the frame so you can carry it to the compost pile and tip it out.

American Lawn Mower Co. makes it under the Scotts name, touting its adjustable height control for moving between grass and hard surfaces. For my own setup, it's the one that I'd likely choose. I move around the country a lot and keep my gear modular, and a sweeper this light and small is the easiest to toss into storage.

Keep in mind that it’s best suited for a light fall of leaves. Plan on more than one pass, and if light debris sails past the hopper, slow your walk until it lands inside. Leave heavy, damp leaf piles to a bigger machine.

Brinly's 42-inch sweeper is built for a thick layer of leaves. Two things lift a deep layer—how many sweeps the brushes make and how high they reach, and it ties for the most in this guide on both.

The brush roll is highly adjustable with 10 labeled height settings. This lets you tailor the sweeper to your desired height based on the density of your leaves and yard and grass type.

While not the lightest tow-behind option in this roundup, the Brinly is on the lighter end of the spectrum, which makes it easier to hitch up to your tractor and also puts less strain on it when full of wet, heavy leaves.

Continuous-contact Double-Helix brushes, geared at 5:1, according to the company, last 2.5 times longer than other brushes. Its clevis fits hitch plates 7 to 10 or 11 to 14 inches off the ground, so it rides level on a low or a high hitch.

Ohio Steel's 50-inch model is sturdy, and its heavy steel build runs across a 50-inch path, which suits a big, open lot with pine needles, cones, and sticks to clear. Against a 42-inch sweeper, the narrowest tow-behind size here, its extra 8 inches cut about one pass in six, so an hour's sweeping takes about 50 minutes.

Its brush shaft runs on sealed ball bearings, so you never have to oil them, while some sweepers' brush shafts need oil every season. The chute (the opening debris flies through into the hopper) is 9 inches across, room for a pine cone or a fist-sized clump of wet clippings. Anything bigger catches on the lip and dams everything behind it.

Its 26-cubic-foot hopper holds about five lawn bags' worth, one of the larger hoppers in this guide, so on a big lot you stop to empty it less often. Behind a 50-inch path, I'd want that capacity, since a wider sweep fills a hopper sooner.

What can be an issue is a hopper bottom that wears through where it meets the ground, so set the hitch height that keeps the hitch tubes level and the bag off the ground. Among sweepers under $400 in this guide, it's the widest.

There are a number of important considerations to make before you purchase a lawn sweeper. Below this section, we’ll cover the following topics in further detail.

Before you shop for a lawn sweeper, walk your property. Note how big your lawn is, whether you have a riding mower or lawn tractor to tow with, how steep the slopes get, how wide your gates are, and what type of debris you’ll be picking up, from leaves and pine needles to cones and sticks.

Consider how you'll use a sweeper, towed or pushed, and if you’re using a riding mower, measure the height of the hitch plate from the ground. Then weigh sweeping width (how wide a strip it clears in one pass) against hopper capacity (how much it holds before you empty it, measured in cubic feet). A wider sweeper will obviously cover more area per pass, and if you have lots of thick, dense leaf cover, you want to make sure you aren’t having to stop and empty the hopper every five seconds.

Look hardest at ground speed and the brush-to-wheel ratio, because together they set how fast the brushes sweep. This in turn affects how much debris is pulled into the hopper in relation to the speed you are moving at. The brushes and how far they adjust come next. You want to make sure you aren’t scalping your lawn with the brushes, but also make sure you can adjust them to a height sufficient to pick up debris. The wheels and weight come last, since they mostly decide grip and the load on your tractor.

A push sweeper suits a small lawn, a patio, or a strip of driveway. A tow-behind needs a tractor of some kind, either a lawn tractor or a zero-turn mower with a rear hitch. If you don't have a riding mower or lawn tractor, check out our buying guides to the best riding lawn mowers and the best zero-turn mowers.

Keep in mind the working capacity of your riding mower. A tow-behind sweeper full of wet, heavy leaves can double its dry weight and put strain on your mower’s transmission. Before you buy, find the towing capacity in your tractor's manual and compare it with the sweeper's loaded weight. One final aspect of weight to factor in is the operator’s weight, which can affect the operating capacity of the mower.

Keep a tow-behind off steep slopes. Each sweeper's operator’s manual details slopes its own way, and there is no universal numbering system. One maker's published figure is 10 degrees, which is a rise of about 2 inches per foot, so read the slope warning for the model you're considering if your lawn has a grade. Your tractor's manual sets a slope limit too, sometimes a lower one for towing, and the lower of the two is the one to follow.

To measure a grade, lay a 2-foot level on the slope pointing downhill, lift the downhill end until the bubble centers, and measure the gap under that end in inches. Half that gap is the rise per foot.

"Fits all tractors" usually means the hitch pin (the steel pin that drops through the sweeper's hitch and the hole in your tractor's hitch plate to join them) fits. What varies is height. Hitch plates sit at different heights on different tractors, and the sweeper has to ride level at whatever height yours sits. A sweeper that tips forward or back changes the height its brushes run at, so they either dig in or skim. Tipped forward, it can also drag the front of its hopper on the ground.

The level check is one you can see. Hitched up on level ground, the hitch tubes should sit roughly level with the ground.

You don't need the sweeper in hand to check fit. Before you order one, park your tractor on level ground, measure from the ground to the bottom of the hitch plate, and compare that with the hitch heights the sweeper's maker lists, checking its manual for where it measures from and how it rounds. If your measurement falls outside every height a maker lists, look for a model whose range covers your dimensions.

Height range is varied with hitch brackets that assemble differently for different heights, a clevis with more than one set of mounting holes, or a hitch with several height positions. Some add an offset hitch, so you can mow and sweep in one pass.

Push sweepers usually cover a path of about 2 feet, and tow-behinds run wider, some to 54 inches. A 54-inch path covers more than a quarter more ground per pass than a 42-inch one, which saves more than one pass in five. On a lawn that takes 20 passes with a 42-inch sweeper, a 54-inch one finishes in about 16, which means less time on the seat and fewer turns at the ends.

Wider is harder to steer around beds and trees, and a tow-behind's frame can be close to a foot wider than its path. Makers list the assembled width in their specifications, so check it, and the height, against your gate and your shed door.

Hopper capacity is measured in cubic feet, and a 39-gallon lawn bag holds a bit over 5 cubic feet. Hoppers run from a few cubic feet on a small push sweeper to 30 on some large tow-behinds, and a bigger one means fewer trips to empty it. Treat the numbers as approximate, since retailer listings don't always match the maker's figure.

Tow-behinds usually empty from the seat, with a rope or a handle that tips the hopper. Push sweepers empty by lifting the hopper off the frame or tipping the whole machine forward. Given the choice, I prefer a dump handle. A rigid handle gives you leverage on a heavy, wet load, and there's no rope to tangle in the brushes. If you get a rope dump, fasten the rope or its pull handle to the tractor and cut off any loose tail, so nothing trails into the brushes or wheels. On a push sweeper, I like a hopper that lifts off, so I can carry it straight to the compost pile.

Because the wheels drive the brushes, your ground speed sets your sweeping power. Drive too slowly, and debris won't carry all the way to the back of the hopper. Drive too fast, and you risk damaging the wheels and gears.

Manufacturers generally cap ground speed between 4 and 6 mph. What I have found to be a smart rule of thumb is to start at a 3 mph cruising pace (covering about 44 feet in 10 seconds), and then gradually speed up, staying under the maker's limit, until the material is reliably hitting the back of the hopper. A 4-mph cap works out to about 59 feet in 10 seconds, and 6 mph to 88 feet. Stop now and then and look at the load. If it heaps up at the front of the hopper, the brushes need more speed, and if light debris sails over the top, slow down.

With your top speed limited, the real sweeping power comes down to the sweeper's gearing and wheel diameter. Manufacturers express this as a ratio, such as 4.5:1.

If you tow a sweeper with 12-inch wheels at 3 mph, the wheels turn at roughly 84 revolutions per minute (rpm). With a 4.5:1 ratio, those brushes are spinning at about 380 rpm. Bump that gearing up to 5.6:1 on the exact same wheels, and your brushes will spin at about 470 rpm.

Sweepers carry anywhere from two to six brushes on the shaft, and more brushes mean more sweeps for every turn. Some makers twist their brushes into a spiral or a double helix along the shaft, so part of each brush is always touching the grass and the sweeper runs smoother over bumps.

Brushes wear out, though, and can be costly to replace, which is why some warranties exclude them. Along with checking whether the warranty covers brush replacement, check that replacements are sold for the model you buy.

Brush height is a buying question, too. Some sweepers publish their range, about 1/4 inch to just over 3 inches, with a chart matching settings to conditions. Others give only a target of about 1/2 inch into the grass and no top height. For a deep layer of leaves, look for a range that reaches past 2 inches, which generally covers heavy leaves.

A sweeper's wheels turn its brushes, so a wheel that slides instead of rolling slows the sweep, and grip on the grass is part of pickup. Most sweeper wheels are semi-pneumatic tires (rubber tires that aren't inflated) or hard nylon or plastic, often reinforced with glass fiber, and none of these can go flat.

Diameter also matters. At the same ground speed, a smaller wheel turns more often, so it spins the brushes faster at the same gearing. At 3 mph, a 12-inch wheel geared at 5:1 turns its brushes about 420 times a minute, and a 10-inch wheel with the same gearing about 500.

On a push sweeper, weight is what you shove and lift. On a tow-behind, empty weight is only the starting point, and the loaded weight is what has to stay under your tractor's rated towing capacity.

Check the brush height first. Brushes set too low drag in the grass, and the wheels skip and slip instead of turning them. Stop the mower safely and go check the sweeper. Then raise the brushes one setting and try again. If the wheels still skid, stop again and look for something wrapped around the brush shaft or jammed in a wheel. If you have to pull a wheel to clear it, follow the owner's manual and take off one side at a time, since the left and right wheel gears often aren't interchangeable.

Some, but it isn't the best job for one. Wet leaves mat down and weigh far more than dry ones, which adds to what your tractor has to pull and stop, and dropping the brushes to dig into a wet mat only makes the wheels skid. Pushing into a wet mat of leaves loads the machine the same way, and a sweeper that already needs a flat lawn or several passes on dry leaves will struggle more with wet ones. Skip the job entirely on a muddy lawn. Sweep after the surface dries if you can, and empty the hopper right away. Damp material left in the hopper damages the bag, and a stored load of damp clippings can heat up enough to catch fire.

Keep the brushes as high as they'll still sweep, which cuts drag and wear on the brushes and wheels. Agri-Fab's 44-inch manual, for example, calls for oiling the wheel bearings once a season, lubricating the brush shaft at the start and end of the season, and greasing the wheel gears every two years. Some manuals call for white lithium grease on the wheel bearings and gears, and others call for light oil, so check the owner's manual before using anything.

Store the sweeper empty and clean with the brushes off the ground. When the brushes leave debris behind at a setting that previously worked fine, it's time to replace them.

#6269. What the Trump administration’s focus on AI and quantum means for science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Research on the technologies is thriving, but some scientists worry about what’s been displaced

On October 8, 2026, President Trump unveiled his administration’s new federal science priorities.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.

These technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” says Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.

In June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.

Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.

Many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” says Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is important, because you never know where some advance will come from.”

Through Genesis, the DOE plans to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” says astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”

This year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.

H. Stockebrand/RubinObs/NOIRLab/AURA/SLAC/DOE/NSF

Other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have launched their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.

Many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” says John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.

Compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” says Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing shows promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.

Accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.

AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston says. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.

In the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.

As excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she says. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.

In response to these concerns, Gil says that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.

Sarrao says that it’s important to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”

Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.
