#6266. The 8 Best MagSafe-Compatible Portable Chargers For On-the-Go Charging

A magnetic battery pack snaps onto your phone and keeps it going all day, no cable needed.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A good portable battery pack keeps your phone alive through long travel days, packed schedules, and everything in between. If you have a MagSafe iPhone (the iPhone 12 or newer) or an Android phone that supports Qi2, a magnetic pack is the most convenient choice: it clicks onto the back of our favorite phones and starts charging, with no cable to carry.

These packs have come a long way. The first MagSafe batteries charged at a sluggish 5 watts. Many of today’s Qi2 packs deliver 15 watts, and the newest Qi2.2 models reach 25 watts while fitting twice the battery into a body about as thin as your phone. Plenty also add built-in cables, kickstands, and fast USB-C ports for topping up a second device.

All that progress means more choice, and more spec sheets that look the same. We’ve rounded up the best MagSafe portable chargers you can buy right now, from slim everyday packs to fast premium picks, so you can find the right one for you.

I’ve used MagSafe battery packs with my iPhone for years. The ones I kept using had a strong magnet and enough battery to get through a day away from an outlet. Most picks here support Qi2, which charges at 15 watts, or Qi2.2, which charges at up to 25 watts on an iPhone 16 or newer. I looked for packs around 10,000 mAh, since that size can charge most phones and then some. I also looked for a USB-C port of 30 watts or more, so the pack itself recharges quickly.

The INIU SnapGo Air packs a 10,000 mAh battery into a body just half an inch thick. It supports Qi2.2 wireless charging at up to 25 watts, and INIU says it can take an iPhone 17 Pro from empty to 50 percent in 33 minutes. That top speed works on the iPhone 16 Plus, 16 Pro Max, and newer models running iOS 26. The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts.

For faster charging, plug in the USB-C cable attached to the pack. It delivers 45 watts, which INIU says charges an iPhone 17 Pro from 20 to 78 percent in 25 minutes. The pack also supports passthrough charging, so when it’s plugged into the wall, it charges itself and your phone at the same time. The cable doubles as a lanyard and detaches, and a digital display shows the exact battery percentage.

For $23, the LISEN Ultra Slim charges at the same 15-watt Qi2 speed as the Anker Nano, which costs more than twice as much. It’s 0.38 inches thick and weighs 3.6 ounces. LISEN says it charges an iPhone 17 to about 50 percent in an hour. Past 75 percent, it slows down on purpose to protect your phone’s battery.

LISEN lists the battery as 5,000 mAh but gives a rated capacity of 3,000 mAh. The rated number is closer to how much charge reaches your phone, so plan on a partial top-up rather than a full charge. Plugged in with a USB-C cable, it charges at up to 20 watts. It only works with the iPhone 12 through 18. LISEN recommends pairing it with a MagSafe case, since other cases can cause overheating.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro costs twice as much as our top pick, and most of that extra money goes toward cooling. Wireless charging creates heat, and many packs slow down as they warm up. This one has a small fan and layers of graphene that Anker says keep it cool, so it can stay at its top speed of 25 watts for longer. It’s rated to charge an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 25 minutes.

Its USB-C port runs at 45 watts in both directions, fast enough to refill the pack from 0 to 80 percent in under an hour. A screen shows battery level, charging speed, temperature, and battery health, and a built-in stand folds out to prop up your phone for video.

UGREEN says the MagFlow can fully charge an iPhone 17 Pro Max more than 2.5 times before it needs a wall outlet. At 20,000 mAh, it holds twice as much as our top pick, and a digital display on the side shows how much is left.

Wireless charging runs at up to 25 watts, which UGREEN says gets an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 30 minutes. The built-in USB-C cable on the side doubles as a carry strap, and UGREEN rates it for more than 10,000 bends. The pack's USB-C port charges at up to 45 watts and refills the pack at the same rate, and a USB-A port lets you plug in older cables.

Fitting twice the battery makes the MagFlow heavier and thicker than our 10,000 mAh picks. That makes it harder to slip into a pocket, and it adds noticeable weight to the back of your phone while it charges.

The Sharge Icemag 3 has a see-through case that shows the internal components, plus a subtle RGB light. It charges wirelessly at up to 25 watts using Qi2.2, and Sharge says that gets an iPhone 17 Pro from zero to 50 percent in 30 minutes. A built-in fan keeps the pack’s surface cool, so charging stays steady. The fan doesn't lower your phone's temperature.

A fold-out kickstand holds your phone upright or sideways for video calls. The built-in USB-C cable and a second USB-C port sit on the side, so you can still hold your phone normally while it charges via cable. Unlike the previous two picks, the wired connection charges a bit slower at up to 35 watts.

The Anker Nano Magnetic Power Bank is 0.34 inches thick and weighs 4.3 ounces, about a third less than the INIU. Because it’s Qi2 rather than Qi2.2, it charges wirelessly at up to 15 watts. Its 5,000 mAh battery is half the size of our other picks, but that makes it more pocketable.

Anker’s own figures show it charging an iPhone 17 to 85 percent and an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 63 percent with the phone in Low Power Mode. That makes it a backup for a long day, not a full refill. A graphene layer inside spreads heat, so the pack stays cool. The USB-C port charges a phone at up to 20 watts, and the pack comes in six colors with a two-year warranty.

If you take your phone on hikes or to the beach, the TORRAS MiniMag Pro is the magnetic pack to get. TORRAS rates it IP54, so it should be protected from dust and splashes from any direction; however, it isn't meant for underwater use.

Inside is a semi-solid-state battery that TORRAS says passed puncture, crush, and drop testing. An aluminum frame wraps the body, and a digital display shows the remaining charge.

Wireless charging tops out at 15 watts, and with a USB-C cable, the pack charges a phone at up to 30 watts. With passthrough charging, one cable plugged into the wall charges the pack and your phone together overnight.

The iPhone Air gave up battery capacity to get its thin body, and Apple’s answer is a battery pack built just for it. On the Air, Apple says it adds up to 65 percent more charge. The pack is shaped around the Air's camera bump, so it doesn't fit other iPhones.

While it fits the Air perfectly, wireless charging tops out at 12 watts. For faster top-ups, leave the battery attached and plug your phone into a 25-watt or higher adapter; the phone and battery charge together. The pack also has no battery readout. Instead, a single hidden light glows green while it charges and orange when it runs low.

Check the box for Qi2 or Qi2.2. Qi2 packs charge wirelessly at up to 15 watts, while Qi2.2 packs reach 25 watts, which Apple says can bring an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 30 minutes. Packs sold as "magnetic" or "MagSafe-compatible" without Qi2 certification often charge at just 7.5 watts.

The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts even on a Qi2.2 pack, so if you own one, a cheaper Qi2 pack will charge it just as fast. For 25 watts, you need a newer phone, such as the iPhone 16 series and later models running iOS 26.

For most people, I recommend a pack around 10,000 mAh, the size of our top pick. Don't expect two full charges, though. Some power is lost in the battery cells and in the circuits that convert it for your phone. Anker says its 10,000 mAh pack delivers about 5,500 to 6,500 mAh to your phone. A 5,000 mAh pack is thinner and lighter, but it works best as a midday top-up. A 20,000 mAh pack can recharge a phone several times, but the extra weight and thickness make it harder to carry.

Every magnetic pack has a USB-C port, which refills the pack and can charge a second device. Look for one rated at 30 watts or higher. At 45 watts, a pack can fast-charge a phone over a cable and refill itself quickly. Anker says the MagGo 2 Pro reaches 80 percent in 52 minutes. If you want to charge the pack and your phone overnight from one outlet, look for passthrough charging.

Faster wireless charging produces more heat, and many packs cut their charging speed as they warm up. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro and Sharge Icemag 3 use small fans to maintain speed. Thick cases trap heat too. Anker recommends a case no thicker than 2.4 mm.

Most magnetic packs are designed around iPhones. Anker and LISEN don't recommend their packs for Android phones, and Apple’s own battery fits only the iPhone Air. If you use a case, make sure it's MagSafe-compatible, or the magnet won't hold well.

#6265. Can robots save Earth orbit?

There are likely fewer satellites in Earth orbit right now than there will be at any point for the rest of your life.

It’s a sobering thought. The threats from our ever-more-crowded skies are well documented: light pollution from megaconstellations, aluminum oxide accumulating in the upper atmosphere as satellites burn up on reentry, and the possibility of a chain reaction of collisions and debris that could render entire orbital regions unusable for generations — to name a few. So what can we do?

One possible solution lies in the emerging satellite-servicing industry — also known as in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM). Satellites can be refueled, repaired, and repositioned — extending their operational lives and reducing the need to launch replacements. The technology has been demonstrated and the industry is expanding.

But unlocking the potential of this technology will also require a sea change in how space is regulated, experts say. “Servicing needs to go hand in hand with regulation to be effective,” says Jonas Bahlmann, a doctoral researcher at the University of Luxembourg who studies space sustainability. Some regulations may need to be eased or eliminated, and others created in order to incentivize the industry to tackle the problem. If done right, new regulations could create a win-win — slowing the crowding in Earth orbit while boosting the bottom line of the launch providers, but it’s a problem without easy answers.

The first spacecraft to undergo repair in space was NASA’s Skylab space station, launched on May 14, 1973. During launch, the station lost its micrometeoroid shield. Designed to protect the spacecraft from impacts, the shield also shaded Skylab from the Sun. Without the shield, the craft wasn’t habitable for human occupants as internal temperatures could become unbearably high.

On May 25, 1973, NASA sent up the station’s first crew with newly designed hardware to replace the shield. Across a series of spacewalks, the crew installed the nylon and Mylar parasol, successfully completing the first on-orbit repair.

Brian Weeden, who directs commercial space research at the Aerospace Corporation’s Center for Space Policy and Strategy, says over the decades since, ISAM has gone through three distinct waves.

The first wave rode the space shuttle. Astronauts on a shuttle mission serviced the Solar Maximum Mission in 1984 and, across five shuttle missions between 1993 and 2009, repaired and upgraded the Hubble Space Telescope. Initially, Weeden tells Astronomy, the shuttle was seen “as a vehicle you could reuse; you could do servicing of satellites and [these] kinds of things.” Ultimately “that never really panned out,” he concludes. Each shuttle launch cost $1 billion, two orbiters were lost in the Challenger and Columbia disasters, and the entire program was eventually retired in 2011.

The second wave, which began in the mid-2000s, swapped astronauts for robots. DARPA’s Orbital Express mission showed spacecraft could service each other autonomously. In 2007, the mission’s servicing satellite ASTRO transferred hydrazine fuel and installed a battery for its counterpart satellite NEXTSat while the two were in low-Earth orbit (LEO). Several other experiments followed, like NASA’s Robotic Refueling Missions on the International Space Station (ISS), which demonstrated refueling of satellites not designed for servicing and advanced cryogenic fuel storage across its three phases beginning in 2011. Still, these second-wave missions were more technology demonstrations than a business model.

“But then about 10 years ago, you started to see this … third wave of real interest,” Weeden says. These new missions draw on three basic servicing tasks — refueling a satellite, repositioning its orbit, and repairing or upgrading its hardware.

Virginia-based aerospace and defense contractor Northrop Grumman became the first commercial firm to service a satellite when its Mission Extension Vehicle-1 (MEV-1) launched in 2019 to extend the life of an aging communications satellite in geosynchronous Earth orbit (GEO). Rather than transferring propellant, MEV-1 docked directly to the satellite and became its new thruster. MEV-2 followed, docking in 2021 with a similar communications satellite.

In March 2021, Astroscale — a satellite-servicing company headquartered in Tokyo — launched ELSA-d, a mission aimed in the other direction: moving a spacecraft lower to speed its reentry for debris removal. ELSA-d demonstrated that a robotic spacecraft could capture an object in orbit, the core capability any debris-removal service depends on. The mission was aborted early due to thruster issues before it could attempt to capture an uncontrolled, tumbling object.

That same year, Orbit Fab, a satellite-refueling company based in Lafayette, Colorado, launched Tanker-001 Tenzing: a technology demonstration that they call the first commercial fuel depot in orbit. Tenzing is a small, 77-pound (35 kilograms), microwave-sized satellite that houses a full tank of storable high-test peroxide fuel and Orbit Fab’s proprietary refueling interface, which is known as the Rapidly Attachable Fluid Transfer Interface (RAFTI). Tenzing has not been used to refuel any satellites, but is one step on Orbit Fab’s journey to make in-orbit refueling routine. The company is targeting 2026 for its first refueling missions and envisions an architecture where shuttles deliver fuel from depots like Tenzing to customers in orbit.

In September 2025, NASA contracted Katalyst Space Technologies, a small robotic-servicing company based in Flagstaff, Arizona, to send its LINK spacecraft to rendezvous with the aging Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and reposition the X-ray telescope into a higher, safer orbit. The mission launched in July 2026. Unfortunately, the craft experienced control issues after launch, and on Aug. 19, NASA announced the mission would not attempt to capture Swift.

Perhaps the most capable example of a third wave ISAM spacecraft is Northrop Grumman’s Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV). Launched on July 21 of this year, the spacecraft is billed as a next-generation on-orbit servicing vehicle. It features robotic arms, developed with DARPA funding, that can inspect a malfunctioning satellite, swap components, and install upgrades. It also carries three Mission Extension Pods (MEP) that it can attach to satellites as cheaper alternatives to a full MEV. Once the first three MEPs are deployed, replacements will launch and rendezvous with MRV. A built-in standardized refueling port will ensure MRV can sustain its mission for at least a decade. The spacecraft will arrive in geosynchronous orbit in 2027 to perform its first demonstrations.

Unlike the two waves of on-orbit servicing before it, Weeden says this one hasn’t lost steam. Where earlier eras produced isolated demonstrations, this wave has laid the foundation for an industry that may soon see companies competing and selling ISAM services. A 2026 study led by Igor Levchenko of the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy and published in the journal npj Space Exploration agrees. They project ISAM turning into a sustained economic sector by 2030.

The study, however, highlights a gap in the industry. So far, projects have been aimed at servicing large, expensive satellites in geosynchronous orbit whose value justifies the cost. But the region with the most pressing concerns about debris, overcrowding, and atmospheric pollution is low Earth orbit — the domain of small, cheap satellites like SpaceX’s Starlink.

SpaceX has handled its debris problem without much need for ISAM. Only two of the roughly 12,000 launched Starlink satellites have broken apart in orbit, each producing mere tens of tracked debris objects. That debris, says Weeden, will “come down within 20 years.” SpaceX designs Starlink satellites for a five-year lifespan and places them in orbits that decay naturally within five years. This is done in part to comply with a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) rule that mandates operators to deorbit satellites within five years of the end of their mission — a rule intended to keep Earth orbit free of debris. But this same replacement cycle also means burning up satellites every few years, putting more aluminum oxide into the atmosphere.

Some forms of satellite servicing in LEO are well within current technological capabilities. But right now, there’s little incentive. Launching a new Starlink satellite is cheaper than servicing an old one, and no regulations are pushing launch providers to do otherwise.

What’s needed is a change in the rules — but that’s easier said than done. The U.S. accounts for over half of all annual rocket launches, giving U.S. regulators substantial influence over LEO. Yet U.S. regulations have lagged behind a rapidly growing industry, say analysts. U.S. commercial space activity runs through three federal agencies: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) licenses launches, the FCC licenses the radio spectrum satellites use, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) licenses satellites that gather data about Earth from space.

That framework dates to the 1980s, built around the industry as it existed then. Newly emerging sectors have shaken things up. “Satellite servicing [doesn’t] easily fit into those existing three buckets,” Weeden says. There is no agency explicitly charged with authorizing servicing missions. Lawmakers have been working to update the framework for decades, but progress has been slow. Weeden calls it a wicked problem, a term from public-policy theory for issues with no fixed win condition.

“It’s complex. It’s never-ending,” he says. If left as-is, Weeden warns, the regulatory ambiguity could scare off investors. Made too restrictive, it could delay missions or push companies to relocate.

While U.S. regulations are stalled in the 20th century, other spacefaring nations have taken steps forward. The U.K., Japan, New Zealand, and France have built or are currently building licensing frameworks for servicing missions. If the U.S. were to follow suit and create regulatory clarity for commercial space activity, those new rules could be leveraged toward sustainability efforts — something that’s already happening in Europe. The European Space Agency (ESA) is pushing for an explicit sustainability policy goal — the Zero Debris Approach, which aims to limit new debris in Earth and lunar orbit by 2030.

As a step toward that, ESA has approved Europe’s first debris-removal mission, ClearSpace-1, which is scheduled for a 2029 launch to capture and deorbit a defunct Earth-observation satellite.

But missions like ClearSpace-1 on their own aren’t enough. While deorbiting space junk eases the crowding in LEO, it does so at the atmosphere’s expense. To address the full suite of problems, sustainability experts argue new regulations will have to incentivize an entirely new way of doing business in space.

In space policy and industry circles, people speak of a circular space economy — a concept that reframes spacecraft’s linear life-cycle. “In circular-economy terms,” Bahlmann says, “we … speak of narrowing, slowing, and closing resource loops.” Design satellites to require fewer resources, keep them in service longer, and recover the materials from retired hardware.

The circular space economy is not possible without regulatory reform, Bahlmann says. In his view, outdated regulations, like the FCC’s five-year deorbit rule, reinforce the linear model.

Bahlmann thinks new regulations should incentivize companies for building satellites with standardized interfaces and modular components that make future servicing possible in the first place rather than restricting them or perpetuating the build, use, dispose status-quo.

According to Bahlmann, this also requires clearer international rules covering who can authorize a mission, who’s liable if something goes wrong, who owns a piece of hardware once it’s dead, and who’s allowed to touch it. Without answers to those questions, Bahlmann says, “it will be difficult to develop a circular space economy if technically serviceable hardware cannot legally be touched.”

A 2025 study published in Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets found, using game theory, that removing dangerous debris already saves operators more in avoided collision risk and tracking costs than the cleanup itself costs.

The problem is that remediators bear the entire cost while operators keep the savings. The study proposes a regulatory fix — a third-party body collects fees from the operators who benefit and pays out to the companies doing the cleanup — win-win.

Another possibility is implementing a so-called international “orbital-use fee.” In a 2020 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, economists modeled what happens if operators paid an annual fee for every satellite they keep in orbit. Each satellite poses a threat to other satellites through the potential cost of a collision — the more satellites launched, the higher that collective cost climbs. The orbital-use fee calculates the dollar value of that risk and charges it back to the operator each year, similar to a carbon tax. This lowers collision risk for everyone. And, the researchers found it could more than quadruple the industry’s long-run value, from around $600 billion to $3 trillion. Another win-win.

These kinds of incentives could also open the door to entirely new ISAM markets. One such example comes from Levchenko’s team. They propose something they call small mission extension vehicles, or SMEVs: cheap, universal, mass-produced servicers built to service many satellites through simple, standardized tasks like swapping interchangeable parts.

The technology to build SMEVs exists. The problem is cost. SMEVs only make sense if they’re cheaper than replacing satellites. Bringing down costs and making SMEVs a reality could be incentivized through orbital-use fees or other regulatory changes championed by proponents of the circular space economy.

“My impression is that the industry will continue to grow and that we will launch more, not less, year by year,” Bahlmann says. In fact, new regulations put in place to incentivize servicing over disposal may encourage operators to launch more satellites. Bahlmann offers increases in fuel efficiency as an analogy: “Driving becomes cheaper per kilometer, which can encourage people to drive more and partially offset the expected savings.”

But he believes growth and sustainability can coexist. “The circular space economy is not about degrowth, but about enabling growth in a way that creates economic and social value without compromising the environment,” says Bahlmann. The question, he adds, is what that growth looks like. “Without the right design choices and incentives, more efficient services could simply enable more activity and ultimately add to congestion rather than help us avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome.”

Wicked as the problem may be, something’s got to give. Bahlmann puts it plainly: “For a long time, the linear approach worked well. We did not have to think much about debris. But it is becoming increasingly clear that we cannot continue like this forever.”

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6264. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

Eagles appear to be hunting and killing adult baboons, study finds. Does that mean they could have hunted ancient human relatives?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eagles can hunt exceptionally large prey, including a baboon that weighed nearly 60 pounds (26 kilograms), a new study finds.

Some human ancestors were smaller in size than modern-day humans and weighed around the same amount as the baboons. This raises the question of whether they also might have faced eagle attacks, the researchers said.

Until now, it was thought that eagles couldn't lift nonhuman primates weighing over 29 pounds (13 kg), the researchers reported.

Scientists made the finding while conducting research in the Sahara Desert in Chad. They found the remains of at least nine adult baboons that had been killed recently by eagles. The region is home to Verreaux's eagles (Aquila verreauxii), which hunt from cliff tops, sometimes in pairs, and have talons with a grip diameter of 16 inches (40 centimeters). Grip diameter is how far the eagle’s grip extends.

The scientists found deep talon marks on the baboons' bones. These marks suggest that the eagles hunted and killed the primates and brought parts of them back to their nests, the team noted in a paper published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

The photo on the left shows an eagle-baboon encounter, while another image (right) features a baboon skeleton with marks of eagle predation.

The baboons were sizable, with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kilograms). The largest of them weighed 58 pounds (26 kg), which is similar in size to some small hominins, a group that includes humans and our close relatives that arose after the split from chimpanzees and bonobos, the researchers noted. For instance, the Australopithecus afarensis individual known as Lucy weighed about 62 pounds (28 kilograms) when she was alive in what is now Ethiopia around 3.2 million years ago.

While eagles do sometimes scavenge carcasses, this doesn't seem to be the case with the baboons. The "severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip," the team wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

They noted that eight out of nine of the baboons in the study were male. This suggests that the baboons were hunted, since scavenged animal remains would not favor a particular sex. Why eagles hunted mainly male baboons is not clear, and the "male sex-bias in our sample is puzzling," the researchers noted. Male primates, such as monkeys, do sometimes defend against eagles by charging at them, the team added in a statement.

There is one known example of eagles hunting and killing a hominin. The "only confirmed case is Taung Child, an infant Australopithecus who we think was taken by a large eagle around 2.8 million years ago," study first author Catherine Hobaiter, a professor at the University of St. Andrews in the U.K. who has studied primates extensively, told Live Science in an email. The Taung Child weighed around 22 pounds (10 kg).

Hobaiter noted that "several of the australopithecine species who lived around 1 [million to] 3 million years ago would be in the same weight range as the adult male baboons in our study" and would have been vulnerable to eagle attacks. Other large predators, such as hyenas and crocodiles, also would have been a threat.

Nowadays, smaller primates, such as monkeys, defend against eagle attacks by traveling together.

"Modern primate species that are predated by eagles spend time in mixed species groups — for example foraging together," Hobaiter said. "That means extra competition for the food — but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost."

Hominins may have done something similar, with different hominin species traveling together to defend against eagle attacks, she noted.

An illustration of a Verreaux's eagle hunting an adult male baboon.

Robert Simmons, a researcher at the FitzPatrick Institute of African Ornithology at the University of Cape Town who wasn't involved with the study, called the findings "fascinating." Eagles "are opportunistic — an old male or a young male baboon dispersing to another troop found on its own can become prey to an opportunistic eagle, or a pair of eagles," Simmons said in an email. In a desert region, the lack of cover can leave baboons exposed.

This is "certainly a rare occurrence," he said. But in this dry desert environment, the prey available to the Verreaux's eagles is limited, which has forced them to take on larger, more dangerous prey than is typical for a 9-pound (4 kg) eagle, Simmons explained.

W. Scott McGraw, an anthropology professor at The Ohio State University who also wasn't involved with the study, said in an email that early "hominins may have been particularly attractive targets because of their relatively small body size," especially infants and juveniles.

"Given their limited physical defenses, early hominins — and, indeed, primates more generally — likely evolved a range of behavioral adaptations to reduce their vulnerability to raptors and other predators," McGraw said. These adaptations may have included living in groups, yelling out to warn others, and selecting habitats that could offer protection from attacks.

Jesús Bautista-Rodríguez, the coordinator of the Desert Golden Eagles Project who has conducted extensive research on eagles, said that the finds were interesting but was cautious about some of the conclusions.

"I am much more cautious, however, about interpreting the remains described in this paper as evidence that the eagles actively killed healthy adult male baboons weighing over 20 kg [44 pounds]," Bautista-Rodriguez told Live Science in an email. "In my opinion, it is quite possible that some, or even all, of these individuals were already dead, dying, severely weakened or otherwise unable to defend themselves when the eagles fed on them."

He also took issue with how the baboons died, saying that more fieldwork is needed to better understand how eagles came across the baboons.

“The punctures and extensive scratches observed on the skulls and scapulae are certainly interesting and compatible with eagle talons and feeding activity," Bautista-Rodriguez said. "Nevertheless, these marks do not necessarily demonstrate that the eagle was responsible for killing the animal. They could also have been produced during the handling, dismemberment and feeding of an individual that had already died."

Hobaiter, C., Akpona, T.J.D., Kopp, G.H., Dominy, N.J. (2026). Signs of eagle predation on a 22-kg adult primate. American Journal of Biological Anthropology. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.70377

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6262. The Blueair 511i Max Includes More Automation Features Than Any Other Air Purifier I’ve Seen

Smaller and sleeker than most air purifiers, it doesn’t skimp on functionality.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s certainly true that good things come in small packages, but with a lot of home appliances, small packages mean accepting a trade-off. In exchange for the convenience associated with a less bulky physical profile, you give up some functionality—cooling rate with air conditioners, capacity with a vacuum, and smart features when it comes to many smaller space heaters and air purifiers.

The Blueair 511i Max, however, is an air purifier that gives you everything you could expect or want in terms of features and functionality but in a relatively small package. While it’s not going to set speed records, especially if you’re running it in a more open space, this is an excellent air purifier for a home office or bedroom. I say this because it runs quietly, looks sharp, and comes with scheduling, air quality monitoring, and more.

Out of the box, the 511i Max is basically ready to run. With WiFi or Bluetooth, you can connect the purifier to the Blueair app. Here, you can turn the purifier on and off, change speeds, and adjust the brightness on the display. This is also where you can utilize the purifier’s bevy of smart features.

First up is the app’s scheduling hub, where you can customize schedules along a number of criteria. You can select the start and stop time, and if you want a particular schedule, you can set it to run daily, on weekdays, or on weekends. You can also select what mode or speed you want, too.

“Welcome Home” mode is one of the features that comes with this purifier that I haven’t seen before. Basically what it does is identify when your phone is within a certain radius of your home and tell the purifier to turn on or off once you reach that threshold. The idea is that it will run roughly 10 to 15 minutes before you get home or after you leave. I wouldn’t say it’s an essential feature, but it’s a thoughtful foray into smart scheduling.

Outside of scheduling, the 511i Max features a filter health report that will alert you when it’s getting close to time to replace it. There are also real-time air quality reports that give you more detailed information than is available on the purifier’s display.

One of my pet peeves with air purifiers is simply giving you a quality reading that’s color-based (for example, blue for excellent or red for poor air). That was my biggest complaint with the Levoit Vital 200S-P, the purifier we named Best for Pets.

That’s what the 511i Max does on the display, but you can get a numeric reading in the app. I find it helpful to know if I’m on the right or wrong side of moderate air, and I appreciate that I can do that with the Blueair, even if I can’t by looking at the unit itself.

When I first looked at the 511i Max, I was struck by how aesthetically pleasing it is. The gray cover around the base of the unit makes it feel less like a home appliance, but it’s actually just another working part of the purifier.

This is the first of four stages of filtration—the pre-filter. It captures larger pieces of debris, which helps extend the life of the filter inside. Over time, you will need to clean the pre-filter regularly, or you run the risk of diminishing its visual appeal. What looks nice unused starts to feel like an eyesore if it’s covered in dust and pet fur.

This also means you need to handle the base more gently than you might other air purifiers—it’s just a fabric cover and the filter. You can feel the ribs of the filter when you handle this portion, so if you’re not gentle with it, you can dent or otherwise damage the filter, and replacements aren’t cheap.

After the pre-filter, there is another filtration layer before you reach the primary filter. It’s proprietary to Blueair, and it uses electrostatic filtering technology to eliminate some particles. This also helps extend the life of the primary filter, and it allows the purifier’s fan to run quieter and more efficiently.

The final stage of filtering is activated carbon, which is meant for odors and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). I ran the 511i Max in my finished basement over the course of several days. My cat’s litter is down there, and there was no noticeable odor while the purifier ran. I also used it upstairs in my house after some kitchen smells moved through the house. The air read as “moderate,” and 20 minutes later, it was back to “excellent.”

Also worth noting is the purifier’s cylindrical design, which, in addition to looking nice, means it pulls in air from 360 degrees. This gives you more options for placement and should allow the purifier to clean more efficiently.

This isn’t the purifier you’ll want if you need to clear air quickly or in a very large room or open space—for that, check out the Coway Airmega 400, our choice for Best for Large Rooms. But for a single room, this is one of the more impressive options out there thanks primarily to its design and collection of smart features.

#6261. What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Kratom is a plant, but souped-up products derived from it can have strong and dangerous effects

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up new versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, says Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

In the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi says. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most important is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” says Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”

Mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, says Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and users are happy to tweak.

As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann says, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

When people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

While 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

What is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving users in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman says.

Sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she says. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she says. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

In July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman says. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will quickly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

“There’s risk with everything,” she says. “I think it’s important to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”

#6260. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6259. Voyager 1 reaches 1 light-day from Earth

At 5:16 a.m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will become the first spacecraft to reach a distance of 1 light-day from Earth. A command radioed from home will need 24 hours to arrive, and a reply another 24 to come back. NASA is asking the public to celebrate by sending the spacecraft a signal on the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

NASA launched the twin Voyager spacecraft in 1977 to tour the giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn, while Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune and is still the only spacecraft to visit either one. Both then kept going. They’re now the only probes ever to study interstellar space directly, the region beyond the Sun’s magnetic field.

Each spacecraft runs on a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, the same kind of power source that drives NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars. Plutonium-238, the fuel source, gives off heat as it naturally decays, and the generators turn that heat into electricity. But because the output fades by about 4 watts every year, engineers have spent years shutting off components and instruments to stretch the spacecraft’s lives. This year, a risky maneuver nicknamed the “Big Bang” turned off several devices in one coordinated move to buy the spacecraft and their remaining instruments several more years of operation. Today, Voyager 1 only runs two of its original 10 instruments, and Voyager 2 runs three.

Voyager 1 is closing in on 1 light-day from Earth (about 16.1 billion miles [25.9 billion kilometers]) — farther than any spacecraft has ever gone. Its twin is about 2 billion miles (3.2 billion km) closer to Earth, near enough that a signal takes about 20 hours to reach Voyager 2.

Voyager 1 lifted off Sept. 5, 1977, two weeks after Voyager 2 but on a shorter trajectory as it was traveling to Jupiter. After visiting Saturn in 1980, it drifted away from the solar system’s planets for good. A decade later, it captured the famous photograph of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In August 2012, it became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, and Voyager 2 followed in 2018. Voyager 2 won’t reach the light-day mark until November 2035. You can see both missions’ exact locations on NASA’s mission status page.

A light-day is a distance measuring how far light travels in 24 hours. At about 186,000 miles per second (299,792 km per second), that adds up to roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion km). For scale, the Moon is just 1.3 light-seconds away, the Sun about 8.3 light-minutes, and Neptune a bit over 4 light-hours. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, lies more than 1,500 light-days away.

At a speed of nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), Voyager 1 is anything but slow. Still, it needed more than 49 years to cover the distance light crosses in a single day.

Astronomy usually asks readers to dim their lights. But tomorrow night is an exception: To celebrate Voyager 1’s accomplishment, NASA invites everyone to flash Voyager’s call sign, V-G-R, skyward in Morse code on Tuesday evening. Use NASA’s automated flasher on your smartphone or tablet. Or grab a plain flashlight and do it manually: V: dot-dot-dot-dash; G: dash-dash-dot; R: dot-dash-dot. Dots are quick blinks of the light, and dashes are long flashes of about a second. Pause between letters.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6258. I Tested Yeti’s New Merino Quarter-Zip—Here’s Why It Could Be Your Go-To Layer

The midweight waffle knit is durable, soft, and naturally breathable.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Last month, Yeti launched its Performance Apparel line—the brand’s foray into down jackets, merino wool layers, and fleece zip-ups. Known for its outdoor gear and lifestyle products, Yeti started by producing coolers in 2006, and has since grown its line to include everything from water bottles and camping chairs to backpacks and coffee mugs.

Here at PopMech, our editors have tested nearly all of the brand’s products, so we had to put the new performance apparel to the test. Beyond branded tees and hats, this is Yeti’s first collection to really dive into premium outerwear and layers. With prices ranging from $180 to $400, I wanted to know if the apparel is as dependable and durable as Yeti’s other gear. Check out my full review of Yeti’s Caprock Merino Quarter-Zip below.

The Caprock Quarter-Zip is made from responsibly sourced 250 GSM Nuyarn merino wool. Unlike traditional merino wool fabric, which twists short lengths of fiber into longer yarn, Nuyarn uses a spinning technology that drafts wool fibers along a high-performance filament. This provides enhanced durability, stretch, and softness while retaining wool’s natural breathability.

During my testing, I found the quarter-zip softer and less itchy than traditional merino wool. The fabric feels loftier and plush rather than dense, which is great for layering and helps it dry faster.

“Merino has more versatility than other natural animal fibers,” Emily Walzer, editor-at-large for Textile Insight Magazine, previously told Popular Mechanics. “It has incredible warmth and durability, and can be spun very thin for everything from a base layer to outerwear. If I were going camping, I’d want merino. It’s just sturdier [than other natural animal fibers].”

As someone with sensitive skin, I would still wear a T-shirt under the Caprock quarter-zip, but the performance wool doesn’t scratch my arms or neck to the point where it’s too itchy to wear all day.

Whether you’re hiking, jogging, or sledding with your family, you’ll appreciate the freedom of movement provided by the quarter-zip’s waffle-knit construction. It provides warmth and durability without feeling heavy or restrictive, so if you break a sweat, it’s not going to make you claustrophobic.

I will definitely wear this style on my cold weather runs when I need breathable warmth. Thanks to the Nuyarn merino, it also has more stretch and shape retention than traditional merino. And for my fellow sweaty friends, wool naturally resists odor, making it a prime choice for high-output activities.

“Merino wool is a semi-hollow protein fiber that traps air, water, and odorous compounds inside, releasing them into the air over time,” Wicker previously told our editors. “Unlike synthetics, which trap water and bacteria, wool allows for the passage of air and dries quickly, making it a healthy choice for socks, underwear, and outdoor activity base layers.”

Like other wools, merino is thermoregulating, so it insulates when it’s cold and manages heat and moisture in warm conditions. Yeti’s Caprock quarter zip capitalizes on the natural fiber's benefits, making it great for days when temps are variable. So far, I’ve worn the quarter zip on cool fall days (it’s perfect for taking the bite out of the air in the evenings), and I also plan to layer it under my winter coat as temps drop this month.

Overall, I think it’s a versatile piece to keep on hand year-round, from everyday errands and camping trips to summer alpine hikes and spring transitional weather.

During testing, I found the women’s quarter-zip to run a little small. The neck opening was a tight squeeze for my head, even with it fully unzipped (I wear a size small). For a more generous fit, I would recommend sizing up. However, if you plan to layer the quarter zip under a puffer or jacket, stick to your usual size for a more form-fitting fit.

Priced at $200, Yeti’s performance apparel is definitely an investment, but with the versatility of Nuyarn’s merino wool, you may never need another midweight layer.

Pregnancy and the postpartum period profoundly transform the brain — yet science is only beginning to understand how that transformation can affect a mother's mental health.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Look closely at the medical illustrations used in textbooks to depict the physiological changes of pregnancy, and you'll notice something strange: The bodies often have no heads. Generations of physicians learned to picture the pregnant patient as a torso — a uterus, a placenta, a growing belly — with everything above the neck left blank.

That blank space is not an oversight by the illustrator. It is a faithful map of what medicine chose to study. We need to move on and create a complete picture of what happens during and after pregnancy so we can develop measures to prevent maternal deaths.

For hundreds of years, we have devoted enormous effort to characterizing how pregnancy remodels nearly every organ and system in the body: the cardiovascular changes, the recalibration of the immune system, the metabolic adjustments — most of them orchestrated by hormones the placenta pours into the bloodstream. That knowledge of what is normal is exactly what lets us recognize and treat what is not, from gestational diabetes to preeclampsia. But the brain, one of the most important organs in the human body, was left out altogether.

It wasn't until 2016 that my colleagues and I published the first study showing that pregnancy profoundly and measurably changes the structure of the human brain. That finding, which we described in the journal Nature Neuroscience, became the seed of my lab. In the years since, a remarkable picture has emerged. The brain changes associated with pregnancy and the postpartum phase are more pronounced, or at least occur more rapidly, than those of adolescence — the transformation we usually treat as the epitome of a remodeling brain.

Today, neuroscientists consider the months of pregnancy and the postpartum period to be one of the most plastic periods for the adult brain. These changes are dynamic; some regions shrink in volume during gestation and grow after birth, while others follow the opposite pattern. They are driven by hormones, tracking with the enormous swings in estrogens and other hormones across pregnancy. And they are long-lasting — some of these structural changes persist for years, and preliminary evidence suggests they may last decades. Or, as folk wisdom has long put it, once a mother, always a mother.

For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank.

These findings raise a question I'm asked constantly: Are these brain changes behind the phenomenon of "mommy brain," sometimes called "momnesia"? It is an effect many women report, and it deserves a careful accounting of its possible causes — among them sleep deprivation and the enormous mental and metabolic load of gestating and raising a human being. We are still investigating, but the data so far point in a reassuring direction: These brain changes are not associated with worse cognitive functioning. If anything, it's the opposite: We have evidence that the women whose brains changed the most were the ones who reported greater well-being and, in turn, an easier time bonding with their newborns.

But not every change is benign. The same plasticity that helps a mother adapt can also carry risk. In one of our most recent studies, published in the journal Science Advances in 2025, we found that certain brain changes were associated with a greater rise in depressive symptoms during the postpartum period. And here is the other side of the coin: A highly plastic brain is also a vulnerable one.

During pregnancy and the postpartum period, that same capacity for change makes the brain more susceptible to disturbances. The window that should lead to learning and bonding, for some women, opens onto suffering instead — especially when society fails to support them, when it doesn't recognize this period as a stage in which women need protection and support from their families and institutions.

The brain changes during pregnancy and the postpartum period are more pronounced and rapid than those that take place during adolescence.

The epidemiological data are as alarming as the personal stories behind them. Roughly 1 in 5 women will experience perinatal depression. In developed countries, suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. Let me say that again, because it bears repeating: Suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. And what happens to a mother's mental health does not stay with her — it ripples out to the well-being of her baby, her family and society as a whole. Advancing maternal mental health is urgent, and the first step is to generate the high-quality data that will let us truly understand the brain transformation that accompanies pregnancy and the postpartum period — to describe what happens to mothers on the basis of science, not personal opinion, inherited prejudice or incomplete medical models.

It is a serious problem, but the solution is straightforward ‪—‬ especially now, in the age of artificial intelligence. The tools of modern data science are extraordinarily powerful, but they are hungry ‪—‬ they need large, high-quality, deeply characterized datasets to learn from and make predictions. In maternal brain health, those datasets do not yet exist. We have blood biobanks from pregnancy, neuroimaging from postpartum parents, questionnaires on bonding, records on breastfeeding — but they sit in separate silos, captured at different moments, never integrated. No resource follows the same women from before conception, through pregnancy, and years past birth, linking biofluids, neuroimaging, neuropsychological assessments, and the social conditions of their lives.

Building that resource should be a priority for anyone who cares about women's health. It is the kind of infrastructure that transformed other fields. Databases like the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative for Alzheimer's disease and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study for adolescence turned scattered observations into predictive science. Motherhood deserves the same — not a footnote appended to the study of something else. It deserves its own chapter — its own public, longitudinal, well-characterized database, spanning from molecules to societies.

For the past nine years, my lab's efforts have focused on laying the groundwork for such a database, and we now have hundreds of participants assessed before pregnancy, during pregnancy, and in the postpartum period. But hundreds is not enough. To do this science properly, we need to scale from hundreds of women to thousands and to ensure, as much as possible, adequate geographic and social representation. My role within initiatives like ENIGMA-Neuroendocrinology and the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative is to coordinate with other outstanding researchers to reach that goal with the highest quality and the greatest urgency we can manage.

None of this requires a scientific miracle. It requires a decision to treat the maternal brain as something worth studying with the same rigor and the same resources we devote to every other domain of biomedicine. For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank. What we need is the collective will, and the sustained funding, to finish the picture.

If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org.

Eighty-five percent of women experience pregnancy at some point in their lives. It enables the very existence of our species. Yet this first step in the process of nurturing the next generation has had little serious, rigorous study — until now.

Susana Carmona's A Mother’s Brain is a landmark in ending sexual bias in women's health. Among her many initiatives, she is building a unique longitudinal database tracking how mothers’ brains change from preconception to several years after childbirth.

Susana Carmona is the author of "A Mother's Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution" (The MIT Press). Carmona is the founder of Neuromaternal, a lab based in Madrid, and is a mother herself. She has led international research projects and published her findings in Science Advances and Nature Neuroscience, among many other publications. Her research has been referenced across popular media from the CBS sitcom "The Big Bang Theory" to the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Washington Post, National Geographic, Smithsonian, and Mother Jones.

#6256. Subway Workers Dug Under a Busy Street and Found an Ancient City of the Dead

Archaeologists say the Roman-era body count is still climbing.

Digging under Calle Hilera, a busy street in Málaga, Spain, is bound to churn up remnants of the seaside city’s past. Officials just didn’t expect those remnants to be the literal remains of more than 1,000 people from the Roman era.

During a project to extend the local metro line toward a future hospital site, crews exposed 984 burial complexes holding the remains of more than 1,000 people, according to the regional ministry of public works, as reported by Sur.

The finds began piling up in the spring. When the discovery was first announced, the metro authority had uncovered 600 burials. Since then, the count has climbed past 1,000 individuals, and officials expect it to keep rising. So far, investigations have revealed a wide variety of burial types, but all of them date from the second to fourth centuries C.E., when the Romans were dominant along the Iberian Peninsula’s coastline.

Although the crews found relatively few grave goods (mainly the expected pottery, coins, and a smattering of personal items), the necropolis, which stretches roughly 1,300 feet, has proven rich in other ways. Mario Muñoz-Atanet, the regional government’s public works delegate in Málaga, told Sur that the number of graves will likely grow as excavations continue.

The burials include tile-lined tombs, table-style tombs, and a range of simple pits. In a few cases, newborns were buried inside amphorae. Many graves were also reused. “We are working on them one by one, tomb by tomb,” Muñoz-Atanet said. “One tomb of each type will be displayed in the future metro archaeology museum.”

According to Muñoz-Atanet, plans for that museum are already underway, and finds from the metro excavations will form the centerpiece of its collection.

The burial site also lies close to where the Nasrid Wall was discovered. That wall was built by the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled the last Islamic kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula from the 13th to the 15th centuries, long after the Roman-era burials. Experts believe that in the second century, the necropolis sat well outside the city but along a key coastal route leading out of the urban center. The site may even have been underwater in the centuries before it became a burial ground.

The excavations have also turned up coins from many different places. According to Muñoz-Atanet, these coins help confirm Málaga’s history as a port that drew people from all over.

That cosmopolitan past is no surprise. Málaga has passed through the hands of many rulers, and the modern city is built atop Phoenician, Roman, and Moorish settlements. Impressive historical finds are nothing new in the region. In 2005, for example, excavations at the Dolmen of Menga, a Neolithic monument in nearby Antequera that is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shed light on the site’s ritual uses. A recent study found that the monument was still in use as recently as 1,000 years ago, which may rewrite its history.

If the past is any guide, Málaga’s next great discovery may be just one excavation away.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.
